The latter generations, when the time of obtaining income arrived, diverged in the administration of education and upbringing, separating the two; those who educated did not know how to nurture, and those who nurtured did not know how to educate. This led to the awards and examinations in schools not seeking virtuous conduct from the local communities, and the errors in discussing classics being divided among various officials under the Minister of Education. Therefore, once one entered the lecture hall, they were forever ashamed of civil affairs. When fathers and elder brothers bore straw cloaks and hats, their younger brothers wore light fur robes. They saw high-ranking officials and noble persons and suddenly rose with reverence, but seeing those with calloused hands and feet, even if they were close relatives, they would feel ashamed and blush. In the period of managing income, later generations separated the policies of teaching and nurturing. Those who teach do not understand nurturing, and those who nurture do not understand teaching. This has led to schools rewarding the study of virtue without seeking it from the local community. The errors in discussing the classics have resulted in the division of the duties of the <term>Situ</term> <gloss>Minister of Education</gloss> among various officials. Thus, once one ascends to the lecture hall, one forever treats the affairs of the people as shameful. There are fathers and elder brothers who carry straw rain capes and hats, while their sons and younger brothers wear light furs. When they see high-ranking officials, they stand up in awe and respect, but when they see those with calloused hands and feet, even if they are their closest kin, they feel embarrassed and ashamed. Although these are men in scholars' caps and robes who speak of the principles of the Way, their actual practice of filial piety and fraternal love is not even as good as that of a person on the street. This is why customs are declining day by day. I request that an imperial decree be issued to the education commissioners to encourage the fundamental and suppress the trivial, and to promote the outstanding among farmers. In all cases for enrolling students, one must require that the youths have known the hardship of sowing and harvesting.

<summary>This passage critiques the separation of education and moral cultivation in the scholar class, arguing that the disconnect between elite learning and the practical lives of laborers leads to the decay of filial duty and social customs.</summary>
<keywords>Education, Siku Quanshu, Filial Piety, Agriculture, Social Customs, Scholar-official, Moral Cultivation</keywords>

By the time of the later generations of the <term>Qi</term> <gloss>Yellow Emperor and Qi Bo, referring here to the traditions of medicine and governance</gloss> and the teachings of the sages, the policies of education and upbringing were split into two. Those who taught did not know how to nurture, and those who nurtured did not know how to teach. Consequently, the rewards and evaluations in schools for moral character are no longer sought within the local community. The errors in discussing the Classics have caused the duties of the <term>Situ</term> <gloss>Minister of Education</gloss> to be divided among various officials.

Therefore, once a student ascends to the lecture hall, they forever feel ashamed of civil labor. We see instances where a father or elder brother wears a straw raincoat and bamboo hat <note>traditional peasant attire for labor</note> while the son or younger brother wears fine fur robes. When they see high officials or noblemen, they rise with distant respect; yet when they see those with calloused hands and feet <note>original: "pian shou zhi zu," describing the physical toll of hard labor</note>, even if they are their closest relatives, they feel embarrassed and ashamed. 

Although such people wear the caps and robes of scholars and speak of the laws of the Way, in the reality of their filial piety and fraternal duty, they are not even equal to a common person on the road. This is why social customs are declining day by day. I beg for an imperial decree to be sent to the Provincial Education Officials to encourage what is fundamental and suppress what is superficial. They should promote the excellence of the peasantry and place importance on conduct within the home village. All students entering school must be sons or younger brothers who have experienced the hardships of sowing and reaping <note>original: "jia se," meaning agricultural labor</note> and possess...

<summary>Zhang Huang critiques the separation of academic education from practical labor and moral conduct. He argues that scholars have become ashamed of their rural roots and manual labor, leading to a decline in filial piety and social character.</summary>
<keywords>education, Confucianism, social class, filial piety, agricultural labor, Siku Quanshu, Ming Dynasty, moral reform</keywords>

# Geese and Ducks <note>original: 鵞鴨</note>

**Old Book of Tang** <note>original: 唐書</note>, *Treatise on Officialdom*: In the Office of the Hooked Shield <note>the office responsible for royal gardens and hunting</note>, there are two Chiefs, four Assistants, and ten Overseers. They are in charge of providing firewood and charcoal, as well as the products from reed marshes, ponds, and thickets, to supply sacrifices, court assemblies, banquets, and guests.

**Lu Lian Zi** <note>an ancient philosophical text attributed to Lu Lian</note>: Chen Wuyu said to his retainers, "When Chu came to attack in the past, not a single person died for us. How sparse this country is of brave men!" A retainer replied, "Your carriages are draped in embroidered silk, yet the men are not allowed to use it even for hems. **Geese and ducks** have surplus food, while the men lack even beans and straw. You have pools of wine in your hall, yet the men cannot get a single taste. Wealth is what you possess; risking death is what the men hold dear. If you will not give what you possess lightly to others, yet you wish to obtain what the men hold dear, is that not difficult?"

**Essential Techniques for the Welfare of the People** <note>original: 齊民要術; a 6th-century agricultural manual</note>: Choose those that sit on their eggs twice a year as breeding stock.

**Comprehensive Examination of Literature** <note>original: 文獻通考; an institutional encyclopedia</note>: In the first year of the Jingde era <note>1004 AD</note> of Emperor Zhenzong, taxes on **geese and ducks** were abolished. The annual fixed revenue was entrusted <unclear>to local officials</unclear>.

**Conversations from the Humble Alleys** <note>original: 巷叢談</note>: In the Yimao year of the Shaoxing era <note>1135 AD</note> during the Song Dynasty, there was a prayer for rain due to drought. The Grand Master of Admonishment, Zhao Xu, submitted a memorial saying, "Historically, the ban on slaughtering animals during prayers only applied to pigs and sheep. From now on, I request that **geese and ducks** be banned as well." At that time, Hu Zhitang was serving in the Secretariat; seeing this, he laughed and said, "He truly can be called the **Goose and Duck** Admonisher!"

**Record of Admonishments and Mirrors** <note>original: 鑑戒錄</note>: On the eastern grounds of the Daci Temple, there is a Life-Release Pond <note>a pond where animals are freed to gain merit</note>. People of Shu <note>Sichuan</note> compete to bring many **geese and ducks** to release into the pond on the Three Prime Days <note>Taoist festivals</note>. Chen Yu wrote a quatrain on the gate, and since then, those releasing lives have gradually ceased. His poem says:
That **geese and ducks** belong in the same flock is known to the world,
Yet the people of Shu compete to send them to the Life-Release Pond.
While they keep dogs and plan for chickens at home,
They do not believe that the monk at the gate is actually a wild fox.

**The Dream of Splendor of the Eastern Capital** <note>original: 夢華錄</note>: At the shops of the Mei family and the Lu family, there are **geese, ducks**, chickens, rabbits, stomachs, lungs, eel buns, chicken skin, kidneys, and assorted offal. Each item is no more than fifteen cash.

**Hong Zikui**, *Rhapsody on the Old Vegetable Garden*: The wheel of **geese and ducks** <unclear>fragment ends</unclear>.

### Peaceful Joy
<note>original: 靜悅 Jingyue</note>
Emperor Yang of the Sui dynasty sent a letter to Zhiyi <note>Zhiyi was the founder of the Tiantai school of Buddhism</note> stating: Your disciplined conduct is solemn and refined, and your mastery of the Dharma leads to **peaceful joy**.

---

### Peaceful and Fine
<note>original: 靜嘉 Jingjia</note>
The Classic of Poetry <note>from the Greater Odes</note> says: What is his announcement? It is that the offerings in the vessels are **peaceful and fine**.
Zhang Heng, in his Rhapsody on the Eastern Capital, writes: The ritual washings are **peaceful and fine**, and the rites and ceremonies are clearly distinguished.

---

### Peace Prevails
<note>original: 靜勝 Jingsheng</note>
Yang Xiong <note>a philosopher of the Han dynasty</note> wrote: In the Great Sound, the rarest voice is where **peace prevails**. It perfectly accords with the human heart and fundamentally corresponds to the distant sounds of the **Heavenly Flute** <note>a Daoist metaphor for natural harmony</note>.
Also, in the Records of the Administrative Geography of the Five Dynasties: Yaozhou was originally Huayuan County. At the end of the Tang dynasty, it belonged to Li Maozhen, who established it as Yaozhou and stationed the Yisheng Army there. During the reign of Emperor Mo of the Later Liang, Li Maozhen's son, Wen Tao, surrendered the prefecture to the Liang. The Liang renamed Yaozhou as Chongzhou and changed the army's name from Yisheng to **Jingsheng**. This is also mentioned by Wan Changgeng.

---

### Managed Overgrowth
<note>original: 理茸 Lirong</note>
In the Record of the Hall of Mount Ge, Yang Renshu **managed the overgrowth**. He was a Daoist master <note>literally "Yellow Crown Master"</note> who understood what was called the **management of overgrowth**.
Additionally, Zhang Yue has a poem titled On Visiting the **Lirong** Temple at Dragon Mountain.

---

### Calm and Bright
<note>original: 靜朗 Jinglang</note>
The Literary Mind and the Carving of Dragons <note>a classic of Chinese literary theory</note> states: When water is still, it acts as a mirror; when fire is **calm and bright**, it illuminates.

---

### Quiet and Solid
<note>original: 靜厚 Jinghou</note>
Su Shi, in his Inscription on Wen Yuke's Bamboo Paintings, wrote: Wherever Yuke went, poetry was on his lips and bamboo was in his hand. His countenance was stern and cold, yet he could make the treacherous become quiet, the restless become **solid**, and the vulgar become refined. Now that we are separated by thousands of miles, his poems can be 
<column-break/>
sought and his bamboo paintings can be requested. However, that which made him **quiet and solid** cannot be brought here. This is why I sigh whenever I see his bamboo.

<term>Zhang Heng</term> <note>a polymath of the Eastern Han dynasty</note> in his <term>Eastern Capital Rhapsody</term> <note>東京賦, Dongjing Fu</note>: "Washing and purifying, <note>quiet and auspicious</note>; rituals and ceremonies are clear."

### Quiet Victory
<term>Yang Xiong</term> <note>a Han dynasty philosopher and poet</note> in <term>Tai Xuan Jing</term> <note>太玄經, Great Mystery Classic</note>: "The great sound is heard, the subtle sound achieves <note>quiet victory</note>."
It truly conforms to human hearts, its profound harmony resonates with the distant **sounds of nature**.

At the end of the Tang dynasty, it belonged to <term>Li Maozhen</term> <note>a warlord</note>, who established it as Yaozhou and set up the <term>Yisheng Army</term> <note>義勝軍, Army of Righteous Victory</note>. During the reign of the Last Emperor of Liang, Maozhen's son <term>Wen Tao</term> <note>温韜</note> surrendered the prefecture to Liang. Liang changed Yaozhou to <term>Chongzhou</term> <note>崇州</note>, and <term>Yisheng</term> <note>義勝</note> was renamed <note>quiet victory</note>. Also <term>Wan Changgeng</term> <note>萬長庚</note>.

### Orderly and Abundant
<term>Hall Record</term> <note>堂記, Tang Ji</note>: "Mount Ge's <term>Yang Renshu</term> <note>楊仁叔</note> is <note>orderly and abundant</note>."
He was a Daoist master <note>黃冠師</note> and knew what it meant to be <note>orderly and abundant</note>.
Also, <term>Zhang Yue</term> <note>a Tang dynasty official and poet</note> has a poem about visiting the <term>Longshan Temple of Orderly Abundance</term> <note>龍山理茸寺</note>.

---

### Quiet and Clear
<term>The Literary Mind and the Carving of Dragons</term> <note>文心雕龍, Wenxin Diaolong, a literary critical work</note>: "Water ceases motion to reflect; fire is <note>quiet and clear</note>."

---

### Quiet and Generous
<term>Su Shi</term> <note>a prominent Song dynasty poet</note>, <term>On Ke's Bamboo</term> <note>題與可竹, Ti Yu Ke Zhu</note>: "Wherever <term>Ke</term> <note>文與可, Wen Yu Ke, a friend of Su Shi known for painting bamboo</note> went, poetry was in his mouth and bamboo in his hand. His countenance was stern and cold, making him formidable.
<column-break/>
Now, thousands of miles separate us, yet his poems can be sought, and his bamboo can be requested. This is because the one who is <note>quiet and generous</note> cannot be brought here. This is why I sigh upon seeing bamboo."

# Imperial Parallel Characters

### Peaceful Joy
Emperor Yang of Sui, in a letter to the monk <term>Zhiyi</term> <gloss>a prominent Buddhist monk of the Sui dynasty</gloss>: Your discipline and conduct are strictly cultivated, and the dharma gate is peaceful and joyful.

---

### Peaceful and Auspicious
*Classic of Poetry*: How do we declare this? We follow the ritual vessels <note>referring to the *dou* vessel</note>, peaceful and auspicious.
Zhang Heng, *Eastern Metropolis Rhapsody*: The vessels are cleansed, peaceful and auspicious, and the rituals are clearly defined.

---

### Peaceful Triumph
Yang Xiong: Raising the bells to produce great sounds, but the silent music is the peaceful triumph. 
It truly accords with the human heart, and its original unity corresponds to the **heavenly sounds**.
Also, *History of the Five Dynasties*, Section on Geography: Yao Prefecture was originally Huayuan County. At the end of the Tang dynasty, it belonged to Li Maozhen, who established it as Yao Prefecture and set up the Yisheng <gloss>Righteous Triumph</gloss> Army. During the reign of the last emperor of the Later Liang, Maozhen's son, Wentao, surrendered the prefecture to the Liang, and the Liang renamed Yao Prefecture as Chong Prefecture, and the Yisheng Army as Jingsheng <gloss>Peaceful Triumph</gloss> Army. Also see Wan Changgeng.

---

### Orderly and Abundant
*Record of the Hall*: Concerning the mountain pavilion, Yang Renshu is orderly and abundant. 
He is a Daoist priest who understands what it means to be orderly and abundant.
Also, Zhang Yue has a poem titled "Visiting the Longshan Orderly and Abundant Temple."

---

### Peaceful and Clear
*The Literary Mind and the Carving of Dragons*: When water is still, it serves as a mirror; when fire is clear, it is peaceful and bright.

---

### Peaceful and Sincere
Su Shi, "Inscription on the Bamboo of Yuke": Wherever Yuke goes, his poetry is on his lips and the bamboo is in his hands. His expression is stern and cold, which can make things seem peaceful and dangerous, irritable and thick, or vulgar and thin. Now we are thousands of miles apart, so his poetry can be <column-break/> sought out, his bamboo can be requested, and his state of being peaceful and sincere is not something one can easily attain. This is why I sigh when I see the bamboo.

# Imperial Edition of the Complete Library in Four Sections
## Volume 100

A son of a wealthy family <note>original: 金之子, literally "child of gold"</note> does not ride near the crossbar of a carriage. A sage ruler does not take risks or seek luck through dangerous means. Now Your Majesty gallops through unpredictable mountains; should the horse be startled or the carriage break, even if Your Majesty holds your own life lightly, what of the High Ancestral Temple and the Empress Dowager? The Emperor then ceased his actions. <note>This passage quotes a memorial advising a ruler against reckless behavior.</note>

Annotation: Ru Chun says, the speed of the horse is like a flash.

In the Biography of Liu Rengui in the History of the Tang Dynasty <note>original: 唐書</note>, see the note under the first phrase.

In the Biography of Li Gang in the History of the Song Dynasty <note>original: 宋史</note>, an order stated: How can we, because of one rebelling general, flee at the first sign of trouble and show fear to the enemy? If the Liao Dynasty retreats and cowers, and if this plan is carried out, then after the carriage returns <note>original: 回馭</note>, the people's morale will be shaken and no one will have a firm will. The spirit of the soldiers will wither, and none will have the heart to fight.

Also see the note under the third section in the Biography of Chen Hongjin.

Those who ride upon the cinnabar of golden clouds and pearly vapors are like me; when my Way <term>Dao</term> <gloss>the path of spiritual perfection</gloss> is complete, I shall depart and ascend to heaven in broad daylight. Eighteen thousand men followed on horses.

In Pan Yan's Rhapsody on the Purple Vapor of the Sleeping Hall <note>original: 寢堂紫氣賦</note>: Traveling to the capital and thinking lightly of a thousand miles; coming from the suburbs of Luo and riding.

In Lyu Xiang's Rhapsody on the Beautiful Woman <note>original: 美人賦</note>: When the Emperor first galloped into the unpredictable, he covered the four seas and became the sovereign.

In Song Zhiwen's Poem Written by Imperial Command in Harmony with the Visit to Sanhui Temple: The imperial carriage returns <note>original: 回王輦</note> to the Twin Trees <note>a reference to the site of the Buddha's passing</note>, revealing the Golden Immortal <note>a Daoist or Buddhist deity</note>.

In Su Ting's Poem Written by Imperial Command in Harmony with the Visit to Sanhui Temple near his Former Residence: The curtains lean toward the place of three drinks, at the gate of heaven <term>hunhe</term> <gloss>the celestial entrance</gloss>.

In Sima Zha's Poem on Observing the Rituals in the Suburbs: The bells, drums, and banners lead the imperial carriage <note>original: 騂騂</note> at the beginning of the sovereign's reign.

In Tang Yanqian's Poem on the Residence of King Qi: Old artifacts from peaceful times; only you have fully depicted the carved saddle.

In Cheng Bowen's Collection of Poems Accompanying the Imperial Retinue: The dragon flanks the sun, the single-horn.

A golden son does not ride a balance; a sagely ruler does not ride into danger, nor seek good fortune through chance. Now, Your Majesty rides <unclear>unfathomable mountains</unclear>, as if a horse is startled and a carriage breaks. Even if Your Majesty takes yourself lightly, what about the High Temple and the Empress Dowager? The Emperor then stopped.
<note>Zhu Ru-chun said: "The swiftness of a horse is like this." This phrase is seen in Liu Ren-gui's biography in the *Old Book of Tang*. In Li Gang's biography in the *History of Song*, it says: "This is merely an order, how can one be timid in the face of the enemy due to one traitorous general? The Khitans will retreat and yield on their own." If this plan were executed, then after turning back, people's hearts would be disturbed, with no firm resolve. The morale of the soldiers would shrink, with no will to fight. Also seen in Chen Hong-jin's biography.</note>

# Ge and Ya <note>Ge (Goose) and Ya (Duck)</note>

## Official Records of the Hundred Officials from the Book of Tang
The Director of the Office of the Royal Granaries and Fodder <note>the Jundun Shu</note> has two Directors, four Assistants, and ten Overseers. They are in charge of supplying firewood and charcoal,
---
as well as products from the reed marshes, ponds, and lakes to provide for sacrifices, imperial court assemblies, feasts, and guests.
---

## Lu Lian Zi
Chen Wuyu addressed his retainers, saying, "In the past, when Jing <note>the State of Chu</note> came to attack, not a single person died in defense. How few scholars and warriors this state has!" A retainer replied, "Your carriages are draped in patterned embroidery, yet your warriors cannot even obtain green cloth for their garments.
---
You have surplus food, yet your warriors do not have enough beans or straw to eat. You have pools of wine in your halls, yet your warriors cannot get a single taste. Wealth is what you, the ruler, possess; risking death is what the warriors possess. If you value your possessions and will not lightly give them to others, yet you desire others to give up what they value most for you, is that not difficult?"
---

## Essential Techniques for the Common People <note>original: "Qi Min Yao Shu"</note>
Select those that hatch twice in a single year to serve as breeding stock.
---

## Comprehensive Examination of Literature <note>original: "Wen Xian Tong Kao"</note>
In the first year of the Jingde era of Emperor Zhenzong <note>1004 CE</note>, the annual tax in cash was abolished.
---

## Collected Conversations from the Back Alleys <note>original: "Wei Xiang Cong Tan"</note>
In the year Yimao of the Shaoxing era of the Song Dynasty <note>1135 CE</note>, a prayer for rain was held due to drought. The Grand Policy Counselor Zhao Pei submitted a proposal: "Historically, during prayers, the slaughter of pigs and sheep has been banned. I request that from now on, these also be banned."
---
At that time, Hu Zhitang had a Life-Release Pond <note>a Buddhist pond where animals are freed to gain merit</note> at his residence. The people of Shu <note>Sichuan</note> competed to bring many <note>animals</note> there on the Three Prime Days.
---

## Records of Warnings and Mirrors <note>original: "Jian Jie Lu"</note>
To the east of Daci Temple, people saw <note>the animals</note> on both sides and laughed, saying, "This could truly be called 'the Counselor'."
---
By the pond, Chen Yu wrote a quatrain on the gate. From that point on, those releasing animals slightly decreased. The poem said: "That they belong together is known to the world; the people of Shu compete to send them to the Life-Release Pond. At the shops of the Mei and Lu families, they sell chicken and rabbit tripe and lungs, eel buns, chicken skin and kidneys, and minced chicken. Each portion is no more than fifteen cash.

# Geese and Ducks

**History of the Tang Dynasty, Treatise on Officials:** The Office of the Imperial Supply <note>original: "鈞盾署" - an agency responsible for state provisions</note> employs two directors and four assistants, with ten supervisors. They are responsible for supplying fuel and charcoal, as well as reeds, cattails, pond items, and marsh products to provide for sacrifices, imperial audiences, and banquets for guests.

**Lu Lianzi:** Chen Wuyu said to his gatekeeper, "In the past, when the state of Chu came to attack us, not a single person died. How devoid of brave men our state is!" The gatekeeper replied, "My lord, your carriage and clothes are decorated with embroidery, yet the brave men cannot even obtain coarse green cloth to wear. You have abundant food remaining, yet the brave men do not have enough bean stalks to eat. In the halls, there are ponds of wine, yet the brave men cannot taste a single drop. Wealth is what you possess, while a disregard for death is what the brave men possess. If you do not wish to give your own light possessions to others, yet you desire to obtain what others value most, is that not difficult?"

**Essential Techniques for the Peasantry:** For planting, use only the eggs of those that hatch twice in one year.

**Comprehensive Examination of Literature:** In the first year of the Jingde era of Emperor Zhenzong <note>1004 CE</note>, taxes were calculated based on annual quotas of currency.

**Collected Conversations from the Alleys:** In the year Yimao of the Shaoxing era of the Song Dynasty <note>1135 CE</note>, during a drought, prayers were held for rain. The Censor-in-Chief <note>original: "諫議大夫" - an official position responsible for offering counsel and criticism to the throne</note> Zhao Pei submitted a memorial stating, "In past prayers, prohibitions were placed on the slaughter of pigs and sheep. Henceforth, I request that the slaughter of these animals be prohibited together."

At that time, Hu Zhitang had a pond for releasing captive animals <note>original: "放生池" - a Buddhist practice of setting captured animals free to accumulate merit</note> in the territory. The people of Shu competed to bring animals to the pond on the three Yuan days <note>the 15th of the first, seventh, and tenth lunar months</note>.

**Records of Mirrors and Admonitions:** To the east of Daci Temple, when the two subordinates saw this, they laughed and said, "This can truly be called a censor's admonition."

In the pond, Chen Yu wrote a quatrain at the gate, and from then on, those who released animals gradually ceased. His poem says: "They are known in the world as a flock; the people of Shu compete to send them to the release pond. Recently, you have been raising dogs and plotting against chickens; I do not believe the guard is a wild cat."

**Records of the Splendid Capital:** At the Mei and Lu families, there were dishes of chicken and rabbit, stomach and lung, fish buns, chicken skin and kidneys, and minced chicken. Each cost no more than fifteen coins.

<margin></margin>
Hong Zikui's "Ode to the Old Gardener"
</margin>

# Pearl and Round-Gem <note>Original: 珠璣 (Zhuji). This term refers collectively to pearls and small, round gems, often used as a metaphor for precious items or literary brilliance.</note>

## Chronicles of Emperor An, Book of the Later Han
<note>In the fifth year of the Yuanchu era <gloss>118 AD</gloss></note>
The imperial decree stated: Although we have reaped abundant harvests in recent years, the people still <note>The text suggests a concern for those who remain in poverty despite good harvests</note>.

## Biographies of Li Si, Records of the Grand Historian
In the Biography of Li Si, it mentions hairpins adorned with pearls from Wan <note>A region famous for high-quality gems</note> and earrings made of round gems. The commentary states that the term <term>ji</term> <gloss>round-gem</gloss> refers to gems attached to the earlobes.

## Accumulated Stores
The petty man lacks foresight and does not plan for the long term. In marriages and funerals, they indulge in wasteful splendor and extravagant beauty, to the point where even messengers and servants are <note>This passage criticizes excessive luxury among the lower classes</note>.

## Clad in Silks
Clad in fine gauze and embroidered silks. The Treatise on Chariots and Clothing states: Scaling Mount Liang to gather awaiting jade; sailing across the vast ocean to finish collecting <note>The text refers to the exhaustive search for luxury materials</note>.

## Zhuangzi
It says: The moon is like a joined jade disk, and the stars and constellations are <term>zhuji</term> <gloss>pearls and round-gems</gloss>. The Discourses on Salt and Iron states: Drawing from deep springs to seek <note>gems</note>, setting traps to seek <note>precious animals</note>.

## Rhinoceros and Elephant
Tribute of beautiful jade and coral from Mount Kun comes from Kunshan. Rhinoceros horn and elephant ivory come from Guilin. From the Seven Admonitions by Dongfang Shuo:

## Admonition of Jade
When jade and common stones are valued equally, it is like stringing fish eyes together with <note>pearls</note>. The Changyang Rhapsody states: In the rear palace, pearls and tortoiseshell are held in low esteem, and <term>ji</term> <gloss>round-gems</gloss> are neglected.

## Poem by Yuan Zhen
Ships and boats carry many expensive goods. A poem by Pi Rixiu states: The Southern Yue region offers tribute of <term>ji</term> <gloss>round-gems</gloss>; Western Shu sends patterned silks.

## Poem by Lu You
A poem says: Alas for the poor man in his coat of a hundred patches; he better recognizes the pouring out of ten thousand bushels of pearls. A poem by Yang Wanli states: From the high cliff of a thousand fathoms,

## Tapping Chess
Round gems. Looking up to see the flying spring pouring from the cloud cave, the water forms tinkling girdle-ornaments and plays music; as it disappears, it becomes <term>zhuji</term> <gloss>pearls</gloss>; as it flies, it becomes snow.

## Tingxiu
In the poem Eating Gorgon Fruit <note>Euryale ferox</note>: The Dragon Palace loses track of dawn, vexing the River Goddess; she nurtures round gems to herald the morning light. Wanting to peck at grain but finding not half a grain, she is only made to fill her jowl with <term>zhuji</term> <gloss>pearls</gloss>.

## Containing Gems
The School Sayings of Confucius states: When Confucius served as the Minister of Lu, the people of Qi feared that Lu would become a hegemon.

## Desiring to Ruin
To ruin its government, they selected eighty beautiful women, dressed them in patterned ornaments, and had them dance the <term>Kang-le</term> <gloss>Peace and Joy</gloss>. They also sent forty patterned horses to the Ruler of Lu. The commentary by Wang Su states: The Records of the Historian calls this a dance melody.

## Bright Gems
Of Wu Commandery. Zuo Si.

## Category of Rhapsodies
Cinnabar, golden flowers, and silver round-gems. Wang Zhongyong’s Rhapsody on the Southern Capital states: The southern barbarians and the eastern streams, weak and flowing, large-eyed <note>gems</note>.

## And
Wang Chi, ten kinds of shame and regret. Along the water's moisture. Wang Lantian. Su Shi's Rhapsody. Beneath the poem pavilion.

### Volume 71, Part 1

**fluttering like flowing water** <note>original: 翩流水</note> —— **the carriage drags a silk-like track** <note>original: 曳練</note>. From the poem by Su Ting, *Attending the Imperial Entourage*, it says: "The clouds and mountains — once seen, they are all beautiful; the bamboo and trees — [are so fine they] cannot be painted."

From Du Fu's *Rhapsody on the Sacrificial Rites at the Southern Suburb*: "The hairpins and robes are elegant and numerous; the wine vessels and platters [are set]." Also, from his poem *Climbing High on the Ninth Day*: "The boundless falling leaves — come rustling down; the endless Long River <note>the Yangtze</note> — comes rolling on." Also from the poem *Gulls*: "Several flocks above the azure sea, their clear shadows [flicker] daily —."

Li Jiayou, from the poem *Remembering the Prefect of Chuzhou*: "I remember Shilong <note>Lu Yun</note> in the guest pavilion, with the clear zither and green water —."

Rong Yu, from the poem *Written at King Song’s Pavilion*: "It must be because there are many partings in this place; even the pines and bamboo — carry a sense of sorrow."

Zhang Nanshi, in his poem: "I gradually feel that upon the traveler's sail — the five-tael <note>a type of vane used to measure wind</note> is heavy."

Han Yu, from the poem *The Basin Pond*: "From now on, when there is rain, you must remember to come and listen — to the sound of it hitting the leaves."

Wang Sunzhi, from the *Rhapsody on the Autumn River*: "The light glow of the evening; the distant scenery — —."

Li Shangyin, from the poem *Fine Rain*: "The mood of the girl from Chu at that moment — the color of her hair was cool."

Xu Hun, from the poem *Sending off a Recluse*: "Without a matchmaker, the paths and roads are overgrown with grass — —; since ancient times, the clouds and forests have been far from the market and court."

Xue Neng, in his poem: "I just regret that the date of return is late — hearing the frontier geese."

Wen Tingyun, from the poem *Kaisheng Temple*: "The road divides the stream rocks among the misty clusters; for ten miles — the wind in the ancient trees."

Fang Gan, in his poem: "The wood falls at the river bank — —."

Zheng Gu, from the poem *Losing Alarm*: "The moon is dim and the wind is sharp, where will one stay for the night? On the autumn bank — the yellow reed branches."

Wei Zhuang, from the poem *Written at Yin Xi’s Residence*: "On the desolate plain, the autumn hall's cypress —."

Lin Tong, in his poem: "In coarse clothes — and a head-cloth; just after finishing with my books, I am too lazy to groan <note>recite poetry</note>."

Wang Anshi, from the poem *Apricot Blossoms*: "A path of weeping willows is sealed with purple moss; the sound of human speech — is in the courtyard."

Su Shi, in his poem: "The white ash is quickly pushed aside to reveal the bright red fire; I lie down and listen — to the snow hitting the window." Also: "In the mountains there is only the old man with the grey beard; for several miles — the pipe [music] sees me off and welcomes me."

Su Zhe, from the poem *East Lake*: "The phoenix trees grow on both banks — naturally forming a forest."

Huang Tingjian, in his poem: "The hidden spring falls into the ravine at night — —."

Liu Ji, from the poem *Song of the River*: "The sky is long and the water is distant, where is the person? The reeds and rushes — — a smear of smoke."

Floating water wheels; fluttering ribbons, as in Su Ting's poem for the imperial entourage. Mountains; looking at them is beautiful. Bamboo and trees; in a painting they remain unfinished, as in Du Fu's "Ode on the Southern Suburbs," where the high officials' sashes are ornate and the wine vessels are arranged. Also, in his poem "Ascending on the Ninth Day," the view of endless falling leaves and the vast Yangtze River rolling onward is never-ending. Also, in his poem on gulls, their clear shadows appear in the sunlight over the sea.

Li Jiayou's poem "Remembering the Governor of Chuzhou, My Younger Brother," recalls the guest pavilion of Shilong, with its clear zither music and green waters. Rong Yu's poem "Inscribed at the Pavilion of the Prince of Song" says one should expect many partings in this place; even the pine and bamboo carry sorrow. Zhang Nanshi's poem mentions sensing the expedition sails rising as the wind shifts in the sails. 

Han Yu's poem "The Basin Pond" says that from now on, whenever it rains, you must remember to come and listen to the sound of rain hitting the leaves. Wang Sunzhi's "Ode to the Autumn River" describes light glinting in the twilight and distant scenery. Li Shangyin's "Fine Rain" poem writes of the Chu girl's state of mind at that time, with cool, colorful hair. Xu Hun's poem "Seeing off a Hermit" notes that there are no paths leading to the grass; since ancient times, the clouds and forests have been far from the bustle of the city. 

Xue Neng's poem says that he regrets his return date is late, as he hears the geese of the frontier. Wen Tingyun's "Opening of the Saint's Temple" poem describes the road splitting by the mountain stream, with rocks tucked amidst the misty thickets for ten miles, and old trees swaying in the wind. Fang Gan's poem notes the falling trees along the bank. Zheng Gu's poem "Loss and Alarm" asks where one can find lodging on the autumn shore when the moon is dim and the wind is fierce, amidst the yellow reeds. 

Wei Zhuang's poem "Inscribed at the Residence of Yin Xi" mentions the barren field and the autumn cypress. Lin Tong's poem mentions a coarse garment and a cloth head-covering; once he finishes gathering his books, he sighs in leisure. Wang An Shi's "Apricot Blossom" poem describes a path of weeping willows sealed by purple moss, with voices heard within the courtyard. Su Shi's poem describes brushing away white ash to reveal glowing red coals, and lying down to listen to the sound of snow beating against the window. Another poem says that in the mountains, there is only the old man with the gray beard, and for several miles, there is the music of bamboo pipes to welcome and send off guests. 

Su Zhe's "East Lake" poem says that phoenix trees grow on both banks, naturally forming a forest. Huang Tingjian's poem says that the secluded spring falls into the mountain stream, silent at night. Liu Ji's "Song of the River" says the sky is long and the water is far; where is the person, amidst the reeds and a smear of mist? 

The *Zhen Gao* <note>original: "真誥", a Taoist scripture</note> mentions the mustard seed.

# Imperial Sanctioned Siku Quanshu <note>The Complete Library in Four Sections</note>

In the Biography of Ruan Ji <note>a famous poet and musician of the third century</note>, it is recorded that he once climbed <term>Guangwu</term> <gloss>the site of the historical fortress</gloss> and looked out upon the battlefield where the Chu and Han once fought. He sighed and said, "There were no heroes in that age, which allowed a mere boy to establish his fame." The <term>Guangwu</term> fortifications are located west of Gucang, beneath Sanshi Mountain. According to the Record of Prefectures and States in the Book of the Later Han, Xingyang contains <term>Guangwu</term> City. The Book of Jin records the Sanhuang Mountains, which some call the Sanshi Mountains. On these mountains are two cities: the eastern one is called East <term>Guangwu</term> and the western one is called West <term>Guangwu</term>.

The poet Bao Zhao wrote: The marching cavalry station themselves at <term>Guangwu</term>, while divided troops go to rescue the northern frontier. Yu Xin wrote in the Stele Inscription for the Wuzhang Temple Sutra Cliff: The city wall resembles <term>Guangwu</term> with its continuous banners; the terrain is like Loufan. Furthermore, the Spirit Road Stele for Lord He mentions: The winged formations form <term>Guangwu</term>.

In the Gazetteer of the Book of Han, there is Mention of <term>Guangwu</term> Mountain. The poet Cen Shen wrote: A solitary boat heads toward <term>Guangwu</term>, as birds return to Chenggao.

<term>Chenggao</term> <gloss>an ancient strategic pass</gloss>. <term>Wuyang</term> Commandery contains Chuqiu Pavilion and the old city of Duke Huan of Qi. <term>Changwu</term> is mentioned in the Gazetteer of the Book of Han under Jiaodong. <term>Zhangwu</term> is mentioned in the Gazetteer of the Book of Han under Bohai Commandery. It is situated on a thoroughfare. Duke Zhang resided here. Eastern States contain <term>Zhangwu</term> County. <term>Zhangwu</term> also had salt officials.

In the Biography of the First Lord <note>Liu Bei</note> in the Records of the Three Kingdoms, it is recorded: In the first year of <term>Zhangwu</term> <gloss>221 AD</gloss>, in the summer of the fourth month, a general amnesty was granted and the era name was changed. In the Biography of the Latter Lord <note>Liu Shan</note>, it is noted that when a ruler passes a full year, they should change the era name; however, <term>Zhangwu</term> lasted three years before being changed to Jianxing. Checking ancient principles, this appears to be a formal inconsistency.

The Gazetteer of the Book of Han mentions <term>Linwu</term> in Dingxiang Commandery and <term>Linwu</term> in Guiyang Commandery. <term>Jingwu</term> is a river that flows southeast until it enters the Huai River at Yuyang, traveling seven hundred miles. The Gazetteer of the Book of Han mentions <term>Zhongwu</term> in Lingling Commandery. During the Jin dynasty, it was called Zhongji. Ying Shao stated that it is now called <term>Zhongwu</term>. <term>Chongan</term> is mentioned in the Biography of Zang Gong in the Book of the Later Han: He led troops toward Jiangxia to attack Daixiang. He was startled by bandits in the Bolang Sands.

### Lightly Turning
<term>Qing zhuan</term> <gloss>Lightly turning</gloss>

### Tang and Wu
The *Book of Changes* states: "Tang and Wu engaged in revolution, complying with heaven and according with the people." This is how they achieved the mandate of heaven and responded to the people. Jia Yi’s *Memorial on the Situation of the Times*: "They placed the world under benevolence, righteousness, ritual, and music, and the influence of their virtue spread."

### Fen Wu (Exerting Military Might)
The *Book of Documents*: "They exerted their military might over two hundred li." The *Classic of Poetry*: "Valuing military might, with the *Ya* and *Nan* music." The Mao Commentary says: "Officials of the Zhou dynasty who respect and oversee these matters are those who manage military affairs."

The *Classic of Poetry*: "He trod upon the imperial military might, agile and..."

The *Classic of Poetry*: "Zhong Bo is valiant and courageous." The Commentary says: "Valiant and courageous, he is now..." "Where is he? Relying on benevolence, he is greatly protected and remains in his place."

translations.T1:
The great principle, the unchanging way shared by the Five Emperors and the Three Kings. The *Odes* say: "With coming grandeur, with stopping solemnity, upholding one another, dukes and princes, the Son of Heaven, reverent." The meaning in the *Spring and Autumn Annals* is that a father is not worshipped in the dwelling of a junior branch, a lord is not worshipped in the home of a minister or servant, and a king is not worshipped in the house of a lesser official or vassal. Your humble servant believes that ancestral temples in the commanderies and states should not be repaired, and therefore requests that they not be repaired again.

### Liu Xin's Discussion on Demolishing Temples

<gloss>Your servant has heard that after the Zhou dynasty declined, the four barbarian tribes all invaded. The Xianyun were the strongest; they are today's Xiongnu. When King Xuan attacked them, the poets praised and celebrated him, saying: "We lightly marched against the Xianyun, reaching Taiyuan." And again: "Swelling, thundering, like a court, like thunder; the glorious Fang Shu campaigned against the Xianyun and the Manjing, bringing them to awe." Thus it was called a restoration. When it came to King You, the Quanrong came to invade and killed King You.</gloss>

<summary>This page discusses the unchanging principles of imperial rule and ancestral worship, followed by a historical account of conflicts between the Zhou dynasty and barbarian tribes, particularly focusing on Liu Xin's proposed demolition of temples and the campaigns against the Xianyun and Quanrong.</summary>
<keywords>Five Emperors, Three Kings, ancestral temples, Liu Xin, Zhou Dynasty, Xianyun, Xiongnu, King Xuan, Taiyuan, Fang Shu, King You, Quanrong, imperial principles</keywords>
translations.T2:
Great righteousness is the unchanging path shared by the Five Emperors and the Three Kings. The Book of Odes <note>the Shijing, an ancient collection of Chinese poetry</note> says: They arrive in harmony and approach with solemnity; the assisting lords and princes attend, while the Son of Heaven <note>the Emperor</note> is majestic and profound. According to the principles of the Spring and Autumn Annals, a father is not sacrificed to in the home of a branch descendant; a ruler is not sacrificed to in the home of a servant; and a king is not sacrificed to among the lower officials or feudal lords. Your servants foolishly believe that the ancestral temples should not be maintained in the commanderies and kingdoms. We request that they no longer be repaired.

### Liu Xin’s Proposal on Abolishing Temples

<gloss>Your servant has heard that after the Zhou dynasty declined, the four barbarian tribes invaded simultaneously. The Xianyun <note>an ancient nomadic people</note> were the strongest, being what we now call the Xiongnu. When it came to the time of King Xuan, he attacked them. The poets praised and lauded him, saying: We struck the Xianyun as far as Taiyuan. It also says: The chariots moved with a thunderous roar like a courtly procession or a storm; the illustrious and faithful Fang Shu went out to conquer the Xianyun, and the Man and Jing tribes came to submit in awe. Thus it was called a Mid-Dynasty Restoration. However, by the time of King You, the Quanrong <note>another nomadic tribe</note> came to attack and killed King You.</gloss>

<meta>The text discusses the ritual impropriety of maintaining imperial shrines in outlying regions and transitions to a historical defense of military action and dynastic restoration by Liu Xin.</meta>

<summary>This page contains a petition to cease the maintenance of imperial ancestral temples in local provinces based on Confucian ritual propriety and begins an essay by Liu Xin regarding the history of the Zhou dynasty's struggle against nomadic tribes.</summary>
<keywords>Five Emperors, Three Kings, Ancestral Temples, Liu Xin, Zhou Dynasty, Xianyun, Xiongnu, King Xuan, King You, ritual propriety, military history</keywords>
translations.T3:

The great principles are the unchanging Way shared by the Five Emperors and the Three Kings. The Book of Odes says: "They come with harmonious dignity; they arrive with solemn stillness. The feudal lords support the Son of Heaven with majestic grace." According to the principles of the Spring and Autumn Annals, a father does not perform sacrifices at the residence of a branch-line descendant; a lord does not perform sacrifices at the house of a servant; and a king does not perform sacrifices for an official of lower rank. Your ministers believe that since the ancestral temples are currently located in the commanderies and kingdoms, they should not be repaired. I request that these repairs be discontinued.

### Liu Xin’s Memorial on the Destruction of Ancestral Temples

<gloss>Your servant has heard that after the House of Zhou declined, the tribes of the four directions invaded simultaneously, with the <term>Xianyun</term> <gloss>an ancient nomadic tribe</gloss> being the most powerful. They are the <term>Xiongnu</term> <gloss>the Huns</gloss> of today. When King Xuan came to power, he launched a campaign against them, and the poets praised and celebrated him, saying: "He campaigned against the Xianyun, reaching as far as Taiyuan." It further says: "The drums resounded like thunder; clearly and truly, Fang Shu led the expedition to subdue the Xianyun, and the Man and Jing tribes came to submit." Thus, it is called a restoration. However, when it came to King You, the <term>Quanrong</term> <gloss>western nomadic tribe</gloss> invaded, killing King You.</gloss>

<summary>This page discusses the proper protocols for ancestral sacrifices based on Confucian principles and presents Liu Xin's historical argument regarding the political state of the Zhou dynasty during the reign of King You.</summary>
<keywords>Five Emperors, Three Kings, Ancestral Temples, Liu Xin, Zhou Dynasty, Xianyun, Xiongnu, King Xuan, King You, Quanrong</keywords>

translations.T1:
<meta>This page concludes the introductory remarks regarding the significance of Master Zhu's method of reading, comparing his contributions to those of earlier Confucian sages.</meta>

Among the things stated here, there are points already mentioned by earlier generations, but there are also insights that the former worthies did not reach, which emerge from the unique perspective of Lord Wen <note>the posthumous title of Zhu Xi, 1130–1200</note>. If one can truly follow and cautiously guard these principles without transgression, then the foundation for investigating principle, fulfilling one's nature, cultivating the self, and regulating the family—extending even to obtaining the right timing to practice the Way and elevating one's ruler and people to the level of Yao and Shun <note>legendary sage-kings of antiquity</note>—will invariably be established through this. How could the practical merit of this be considered shallow? 

Furthermore, I would suggest that while the sages and worthies of old did indeed speak of reading, the instruction for people to read books in order to investigate principle became even more urgent with Lord Wen. The great scholars of the Guan and Luo regions <note>referring to the Northern Song Neo-Confucian masters such as the Cheng brothers and Zhang Zai</note> also spoke of methods for reading, but the specific emphasis on following a set sequence, attaining refinement, and first reading what is easily understood began with the Master <note>Zhu Xi</note>. This "greater urgency" is like Confucius speaking frequently of the word "Benevolence" <note>term: Ren</note>. These initial insights are comparable to Mencius's work on the goodness of human nature and the cultivation of vital energy <note>term: Qi</note>. Students especially must not fail to understand this.

<summary>The text argues that Zhu Xi’s specific methods for reading—such as following a proper sequence—provide a necessary and unique foundation for Neo-Confucian self-cultivation and governance. It compares Zhu Xi’s contributions to the foundational teachings of Confucius and Mencius.</summary>
<keywords>Zhu Xi, Neo-Confucianism, reading methods, investigating principle, self-cultivation, Mencius, Confucius, Four Treasuries</keywords>

## Yellow Crane Tower

The Yellow Crane Tower is in present-day Wuchang. The Tang Dynasty's *Tu Jing* <gloss>Illustrated Gazetteer</gloss> states that Fei Wenyi ascended to immortality, riding a yellow crane, and rested here upon his return. Zhang Nanxuan said that the Yellow Crane (Huang He) got its name from a mountain. Today, there is a mountain next to the Yellow Crane Tower called Mount Huang Gu <gloss>Yellow Swan</gloss>. Nanxuan's explanation is correct. According to Cai Heng, a gu <gloss>鵠, swan</gloss> is often white like a phoenix; the *Suoyin* <gloss>Commentary on the Shiji</gloss> states that <term>honggu</term> <gloss>鴻鵠, swan or goose</gloss> is one bird, like a phoenix, implying that a gu <gloss>鵠</gloss> is a type of phoenix. Sometimes it is called <term>hong</term> <gloss>鴻, wild goose</gloss>, sometimes <term>bai</term> <gloss>白, white</gloss>, sometimes <term>huang</term> <gloss>黃, yellow</gloss>. Yellow and white are similar in color. <term>Hong</term> <gloss>鴻</gloss> refers to something large. The *Sijiu* <gloss>Commentary on the Rites of Zhou</gloss> annotation states that <term>gu</term> <gloss>鵠</gloss> refers to small birds like wild geese that are difficult to shoot. The *Yupian* <gloss>Jade Chapters dictionary</gloss> states that <term>yangu</term> <gloss>鴈鵠, swan</gloss> is a gu <gloss>鵠</gloss>, a bird that knows when to come, like the <term>linggu</term> <gloss>靈鵠, divine swan</gloss> today. Thus <term>yangu</term> <gloss>鴈鵠</gloss> is a bird.

## Yellow Crane Tower

The Yellow Crane Tower is located in present-day Wuchang. The Tang Dynasty Illustrated Treatises <note>original: "Tu Jing"</note> state that Fei Wenyi <note>a legendary figure often identified with the immortal Fei Yi</note> ascended to immortality and rode a yellow crane back to rest at this spot. Zhang Nanxuan <note>the Song dynasty scholar Zhang Shi</note> said that the Yellow Crane Tower was named after the mountain. Near the current Yellow Crane Tower, there is a mountain named Yellow Swan <note>term: Huanggu</note>. Nanxuan’s explanation is correct. Regarding the swan <note>term: gu</note>, Cai Heng says that many phoenixes are white, and these are called <term>gu</term> <gloss>swans</gloss>. The Suoyin commentary <note>a commentary on the Records of the Grand Historian</note> says that the <term>hong</term> <gloss>wild goose</gloss> and <term>gu</term> <gloss>swan</gloss> are a single type of bird, much like the male and female phoenix <note>term: fenghuang</note>. Therefore, the swan is of the phoenix species. It is sometimes called "great" <note>term: hong</note>, sometimes "white," and sometimes "yellow." Yellow and white are similar colors. "Great" refers to its size. The commentary on the Superintendent of Furs <note>a section of the Rites of Zhou</note> says that the swan refers to a small bird among the geese that is difficult to hit with an arrow. The Jade Chapters <note>term: Yupian, an early dictionary</note> state that the <term>yangu</term> <gloss>goose-swan</gloss> is a swan; it is a bird that knows what is coming. The "spiritual swan" of today is this goose-swan.

## Yellow Crane Tower

The Yellow Crane Tower is located in present-day <term>Wuchang</term>. The Tang Dynasty <term>Tujing</term> <gloss>Illustrated Classics</gloss> state that <term>Fei Wenwei</term> attained immortality, rode a yellow crane, and returned to rest at this site. <term>Zhang Nanxuan</term> says the Yellow Crane takes its name from the mountain. Today, there is a mountain beside the Yellow Crane Tower named <term>Huanghu</term> <gloss>Yellow Swan/Crane</gloss>. <term>Nanxuan</term>’s explanation is correct. 

Upon examination, <term>Cai Heng</term> states that many phoenixes are white. The <term>Suoyin</term> <gloss>Explanation of Obscurities</gloss> says the <term>honghu</term> <gloss>swan/large bird</gloss> is a single species of bird, similar to the phoenix. If this is so, then the <term>hu</term> is of the phoenix family. Some refer to it as <term>hong</term>, others as white, and others as yellow. Yellow and white are similar in color. The <term>hong</term> is large. The commentary on the <term>Siqiu</term> <gloss>Officer of Furs</gloss> notes that the <term>hu</term> is a small bird of the goose family that is difficult to hit with arrows. The <term>Yupian</term> <gloss>Jade Encyclopedia</gloss> states that the <term>yanhu</term> <gloss>goose-swan</gloss> is a bird that knows when to arrive; today’s <term>linghu</term> <gloss>spirit swan</gloss> is an <term>yanhu</term>.

Monthly offerings to the ancestors and the <term>la</term> <gloss>year-end sacrifice</gloss> for the hundred spirits. During the four seasonal transitions <note>the four days marking the start of spring, summer, autumn, and winter</note> and the days governed by the Earth King, sacrifices are made to the Five Sacred Peaks, the Strongholds, the Seas, and the Great Rivers. In the second month of spring and the second month of autumn, on the first <term>wu</term> <gloss>fifth branch</gloss> day, the <term>shidian</term> <gloss>release of offerings</gloss> ceremony is performed for King Wucheng <note>the posthumous title for Jiang Ziya, the patron of military affairs</note>.

On the <term>chen</term> <gloss>fifth branch</gloss> day after the Beginning of Autumn, sacrifices are made to the Spirit Star <note>associated with agriculture</note>. In the last month of summer, on the day of the Earth King, sacrifices are made to the Central Skylight <note>the spirit of the inner court or household</note>. 詩亡者雅頌之詩亡也既以平王之詩為國風
則是下列於諸侯矣然春秋或書天王者所以
存王道也○鄭氏樵曰七月者西周之風黍離
者東周之風○朱子語類問王風是他風如此
不是降為國風曰其辭語可見風多出於在下
之人雅乃士大夫所作雅雖有刺而其辭與風
異○陳氏埴曰雅詩多是朝會燕饗樂章或是
公卿大夫規諫獻納之所作東遷以後朝廷既
無制作公卿又無獻納故雅詩遂亡獨有民俗

The scope of inner transformation <note>referring to the moral influence of the King</note> and its reach were similar to those of the feudal lords. Since poetry is created based on the state of government, the distinction between the <term>Feng</term> <gloss>Lessons from the States/Customs</gloss> and the <term>Ya</term> <gloss>Odes/Elegantiae</gloss> is tied to the breadth or narrowness of that government. Although the King’s rank is supreme, because his political influence had narrowed, his poems were entered into the <term>Feng</term> category. The creation of the <term>Feng</term> and <term>Ya</term> follows its own natural mechanism; it does not mean that after the poems were collected, they were intentionally demoted.

Master Zhang <note>Zhang Zai, a Neo-Confucian philosopher</note> said: The reason the Royal domain <note>the <term>Wang Feng</term></note> is placed after the state of Wei is for fear of confusing it with the <term>Er Nan</term> <gloss>Two Nan sections: Zhou Nan and Zhao Nan</gloss>; thus, the three Wei states are used to separate them.

Master Cao Cuizhong said: The writing of the <term>Chunqiu</term> <gloss>Spring and Autumn Annals</gloss> began with Duke Yin. The first year of Duke Yin was the forty-ninth year of King Ping. When the world no longer had a true King, the recording of the "First Year" was relegated to the state of Lu; therefore, it is said that "the traces of the King were extinguished, and the Odes ceased."

Master Ji Cheng said: When Mencius spoke of "the Odes ceasing," he meant the Odes of the <term>Ya</term> and <term>Sot</term> <gloss>Hymns</gloss> sections. Since the poems of King Ping were treated as <term>Guo Feng</term> <gloss>Lessons from the States</gloss>, he was categorized alongside the feudal lords. However, the <term>Spring and Autumn Annals</term> occasionally record "The Heavenly King" as a way to preserve the Kingly Way.

Master Zheng Qiao said: The poem "Seventh Month" <note>Qi Yue</note> represents the customs of Western Zhou. The poem "Sorghum in Bloom" <note>Shu Li</note> represents the customs of Eastern Zhou.

In the <term>Zhu Zi Yu Lei</term> <gloss>Classified Conversations of Master Zhu Xi</gloss>, it was asked: The <term>Wang Feng</term> <gloss>Royal Odes</gloss> are categorized this way, but does it mean they were demoted to the level of <term>Guo Feng</term>? He replied: Their language shows that these customs mostly emerged from the common people below. The <term>Ya</term> were composed by the scholar-officials. Although the <term>Ya</term> contain criticisms, their language differs from the <term>Feng</term>.

Master Chen Zhi said: The <term>Ya</term> poems are mostly musical scores for court assemblies and banquets, or works of admonition and contribution by high officials and ministers. After the eastward move <note>the shift to the Eastern Zhou period</note>, the court no longer produced such works, and the high officials no longer made such contributions; thus, the <term>Ya</term> poetry perished. Only the folk customs remained.

<summary>Scholars discuss why the poetry of the Royal House was categorized as local customs rather than courtly odes after the decline of the Zhou King's authority. They examine the historical transition from Western to Eastern Zhou and the resulting changes in poetic style and political status.</summary>
<keywords>Book of Odes, Wang Feng, King Ping, Zhu Xi, Spring and Autumn Annals, Zhou Dynasty, poetic categorization, Confucian commentary</keywords>

The extent of their internal refinement is similar to that of the feudal lords. The <term>Shi</term> <gloss>Book of Songs</gloss> is composed based on governance; the <term>Feng</term> <gloss>Airs</gloss> and <term>Ya</term> <gloss>Odes</gloss> are tied to the breadth of governance. Although the royal rank is honored, it is categorized into the <term>Feng</term> because the governance is narrow. The composition of the <term>Feng</term> and <term>Ya</term> naturally has its origins; it is not the case that because the poems were collected, they were therefore demoted. 

Master Zhang said: The reason the Odes of Wang follow those of Wei is the fear of confusion with the two <term>Nan</term> <gloss>Southern sections of the Airs</gloss>, so the three [Odes of] Wei are placed between them. 

The Cao family, Cuizhong, said: The compilation of the <term>Chunqiu</term> <gloss>Spring and Autumn Annals</gloss> begins with Duke Yin. The first year of Duke Yin is the forty-ninth year of King Ping. With no king in the world, the era was anchored in the state of Lu; thus it is said that when the traces of the kings vanished, the <term>Shi</term> was lost. 

The Ji family, Cheng, said: What Mencius meant by the loss of the <term>Shi</term> is that the <term>Ya</term> and <term>Song</term> <gloss>Hymns</gloss> were lost. Since the poems of King Ping are classified as <term>Guofeng</term> <gloss>Airs of the States</gloss>, they are ranked below the feudal lords. However, the <term>Chunqiu</term> sometimes records the "Heavenly King," which is the way of preserving the Royal Way. 

Master Zheng, Qiao, said: The *July* poem is an Air of the Western Zhou, and the *Shuli* poem is an Air of the Eastern Zhou. 

In the *Classified Conversations of Master Zhu* <note>original: "Zhuzi Yulei"</note>, someone asked: The Odes of Wang are like other Airs, does this not mean they were downgraded to the status of <term>Guofeng</term>? Master Zhu replied: The language itself shows this. The <term>Feng</term> mostly come from those in lower positions, whereas the <term>Ya</term> were composed by scholar-officials. Although the <term>Ya</term> contain satires, their language differs from the <term>Feng</term>. 

Master Chen, Zhi, said: The <term>Ya</term> poems were mostly musical compositions for court assemblies and banquets, or works composed by dukes, ministers, and high officials for remonstrance or submission. After the move to the east, the imperial court ceased producing such works, and officials no longer submitted them. Therefore, the <term>Ya</term> poems were lost, and only the folk customs <unclear>remained.</unclear>

<summary>This text discusses the classification of the Odes of Wang within the Book of Songs, debating whether their inclusion in the Airs of the States signifies a decline in royal status or a reflection of the changing political climate during the transition from Western to Eastern Zhou.</summary>
<keywords>Book of Songs, Shi, Feng, Ya, Song, King Ping, Duke Yin, Zhou dynasty, political legitimacy</keywords>

# 澤哉
或曰序說亦通宜更詳之也
君子遭亂相招為

# How Plentiful
<note>This heading likely refers to the title or a key phrase of the poem being discussed.</note>
Some say that the explanation provided in the Preface is also acceptable and should be examined in greater detail. It suggests that a gentleman, encountering a time of disorder, invites others to seek office for the sake of a salary <term>lu shi</term> <gloss>employment for pay rather than ambition</gloss> merely to preserve their lives and avoid harm. Fu Guang <note>A Southern Song dynasty scholar and disciple of Zhu Xi</note> says: The Master <note>referring to Zhu Xi</note> thought this poem might also have been written by a woman, similar to the previous chapter. This is because both poems begin with the phrase "The Gentleman" and are closely linked in sequence. This interpretation does not harm the meaning, yet how do we know this sequence is not simply a coincidence? Therefore, he also included the alternative theory that the Preface's explanation is acceptable and should be studied further, perhaps wishing to retain the traditional view.

# Collected Explanations
Mao Chang <note>A Han dynasty scholar known for his commentary on the Classics</note> says: "By" <note>original: 由; you</note> means "to use." The Son of Heaven uses the South of Zhou songs, and the feudal lords use the South of Shao songs. Kong Yingda <note>A Tang dynasty scholar</note> says: "The Great Chamber" <note>original: 路寢; lu qin</note> refers to the usual place for performing music. A ruler of a state has music for the inner chambers. Both the Son of Heaven and the feudal lords possess music specifically for the inner chambers. A gentleman serving for a salary in a low-ranking position calls out to his friends. This friend of the gentleman describes the act of being called, saying that there is a gentleman occupying a position in the

# Office of Music
With his left hand, he holds the reeds of the mouth organ <term>sheng huang</term> <gloss>a free-reed wind instrument</gloss>, and with his right hand, he beckons me. From this position within the office of inner-chamber music, he suggests that since the Way and its teachings are not being practiced, they might as well enjoy themselves in this manner. Hu Yigui <note>A Yuan dynasty scholar</note> says: Master Zhu’s <note>Zhu Xi</note>

# Initial Interpretation
states that the gentleman knows the Way cannot be practiced, so he takes an office to escape poverty. Therefore, he accepts a lowly position despite his high character and accepts a small salary despite his merit. These men call to one another to seek salaried office. Although they serve in the lowly role of musicians, they appear joyful and 

# Contented
as if they truly find happiness in this. Their plan to preserve their lives and stay far from harm is profound. Although this is not the ideal "coming forth or withdrawing" <note>referring to the Confucian standard for entering or leaving government service</note> practiced by sages, it is better than those who do not measure their own strength and succumb to greed and ruin.

<summary>This page contains scholarly commentaries on the poem Junzi Yang Yang from the Classic of Poetry, debating whether the poem depicts a woman's perspective or gentlemen seeking refuge in lowly musical offices during times of political decline.</summary>

<meta>continues from previous page: The commentary on the "Junzi Yangyang" poem.</meta>
<header>Imperial Collection of the Four Treasuries</header>

<margin>The Preface says, "The gentleman is at ease, lamenting for the Zhou."</margin>

# Zezai <gloss>The Marsh</gloss>
Some say the Preface is also acceptable and should be explained in greater detail. 
The gentleman, encountering chaos, invites his peers to take up minor official posts to protect their bodies and avoid harm. 

○ Master Fu Guang says: My teacher <note>referring to Zhu Xi</note> suggests this poem may also have been written by the woman from the previous piece, as both poems begin by mentioning the "gentleman" and are connected in theme. While this does not harm the meaning, how can one know it was not merely a coincidence? Therefore, I have included the alternative perspective, suggesting that the Preface is also acceptable and deserves more detailed explanation, as it seeks to preserve the old tradition.

# Collected Commentaries
Mao Chang says: "You" means to use. The Son of Heaven uses the <term>Zhou Nan</term> <gloss>songs of southern Zhou</gloss>, and the feudal lords use the <term>Shao Nan</term> <gloss>songs of southern Shao</gloss>. 
Da <note>referring to Zheng Da</note> says: This refers to the music commonly used in the inner chambers <note>private quarters of the palace</note>. The ruler of a state has music for the inner chambers. 

○ Kong Yingda says: Both the Son of Heaven and the feudal lords have music for the inner chambers. 
The "gentleman" takes a minor official post and calls upon his friends. This poem describes the gentleman's friend, detailing how he calls him. It speaks of the gentleman being in a position of musical office.

# Position of the Office
Holding the <term>sheng-huang</term> <gloss>reed pipe instruments</gloss> in his left hand, he beckons me with his right. Using this music for the inner chambers, the office of the musician, implies that the Way and virtue are not being practiced, so they merely amuse themselves together. 

○ Hu Yigui says: Master Zhu’s initial interpretation states that the gentleman knows the Way is not being practiced, yet he takes office due to poverty. This explains why he occupies a humble position, leaves wealth behind to live in poverty, and invites others to take minor posts. Although he is subservient to the humble position of a musician, he is at ease and content.

# If he is
Truly finding joy in this, his plan to preserve his life and avoid harm is profound. Although this is not the upright manner of a sage or worthy in choosing whether to serve or withdraw, it is still better than those who do not measure their own strength, greedily seeking profit until they destroy themselves.

<summary>This page presents scholarly commentary on the poem "Junzi Yangyang," discussing the role of "inner chamber" music and the ethics of taking minor official positions during times of political chaos.</summary>
<keywords>Zhou Nan, Shao Nan, Confucian ethics, inner chamber music, Zhu Xi, official life, Junzi</keywords>

The gentleman, employed in a humble official position, calls out to his friends. Holding the <term>sheng</term> <gloss>mouth organ</gloss> and <term>huang</term> <gloss>free-reed instrument</gloss> in his left hand, and beckoning me with his right, using this music for the inner chambers, in an official position. Although serving in the humble position of a musician, they are <term>yangyang</term> <gloss>radiant and content</gloss>, as if truly finding joy in this. Their plan for preserving themselves and avoiding harm is profound. <summary>This page presents various interpretations of a poem, particularly focusing on the meaning of "gentleman" and "official employment" during times of unrest. <meta>This page contains textual criticism and collation notes for the Book of Rites (Liji), specifically regarding the education of the heir apparent in the royal academy.</meta>

# Supplement to the Explanations of the Text
# Volume 132

Regarding the term <term>li</term> <gloss>to oversee</gloss>, it refers to inspection. In some versions, this is written as <term>geng</term> <gloss>to change</gloss>, meaning to approach or preside over. <gloss>Leaf 5</gloss> The character <term>geng</term> is also written as <term>li</term>.

->From "In all education of the heir apparent" to "the books are kept in the Higher School"<-

Investigation of Variations: In the Ancient Version, the commentary for the phrase "each of the four seasons has its appropriate study" lacks the character <term>suo</term> <gloss>that which</gloss>. The Song Edition and the Ashikaga Edition are the same in this regard.

Regarding the passage "rising to the school," after the phrase "dancing with feathers and blowing the flute" and after "to spread the poems with silk," both instances include the character <term>ye</term> <gloss>a grammatical particle indicating a conclusion</gloss>.

The term <term>gan</term> <gloss>shield</gloss> refers to a shield; the character is written as <term>dun</term> <note>original: 楯</note>. Regarding the phrase "achievements are easily completed," the Song Edition lacks the character <term>cheng</term> <gloss>completed</gloss>. The sub-commentary notes that this section is actually the second section. <gloss>Leaf 7, right side, line 6</gloss> In the Song Edition, the word <term>huan</term> <gloss>return</gloss> appears after the word "section." In the phrase "must each follow what is appropriate for the four seasons" <gloss>line 8</gloss>, the word "follow" <note>original: 遂</note> is written as "pursue" <note>original: 逐</note>. In the phrase "rising to the school," it refers to the Great School. <gloss>Leaf 7, left side, line 1</gloss> The character <term>da</term> <gloss>great</gloss> is written as <term>ru</term> <gloss>enter</gloss>.

Regarding the citation of the Odes of Zheng, "the left hand holds the flute" <gloss>line 9</gloss>, the phrase "citing Zheng" is written as "Zheng cites." Therefore, he is called the Great Director of Music.

Regarding Ritual, there was Master Gaotang <note>Gaotang Sheng, a scholar who preserved the Rites of Yi during the early Han dynasty</note>; for Music, there was the Zhi clan <note>hereditary masters of music</note>; for Poetry, there was Master Mao <note>Mao Heng, responsible for the Mao edition of the Classic of Poetry</note>; and for History, there was Master Fu <note>Fu Sheng, who hid the Book of Documents in a wall to save it from the Qin book burning</note>. Furthermore, it is said that whenever the <term>Shidian</term> <gloss>libation sacrifice to ancient sages</gloss> is performed, there must be a combination <note>a joint sacrifice to multiple figures</note>. The commentators say: if the Zhou have the Duke of Zhou and the Lu have Confucius, they each perform their own libation separately without combining them. 

As for sacrificing to the former worthies at the Western School <note>an educational institution for elderly commoners and princes</note> or sacrificing to the ancestors of music at the Hall of the Blind <note>the music school where blind musicians practiced</note>, the transmitters of these traditions also say that one sacrifices to the Former Teachers according to the specific field of study. However, the Duke of Zhou and Confucius are not the exclusive property of the Zhou and Lu states. If every classic established its own separate master, how could the Zhou administrative codes have allowed such a thing?

In ancient times, the people regarded the Ruler as their Teacher. Whether the people were benevolent or lowly, long-lived or short-lived, the Ruler was truly in charge of these matters. The officials then assisted the Ruler to serve as mentors and protectors of the ten thousand people. Before the time of Confucius, those called Sages or Worthies, who possessed the Way and Virtue, never failed to occupy prominent positions while living and were honored with the <term>Dazheng</term> <gloss>great winter sacrifice</gloss> after death. These matters are not within the scope of mere students <unclear>to determine</unclear>.

Sacrifice in the Ancestral Temple <note>literally the temple of the First Son, referring to the primary lineage temple</note> is also called the <term>Di</term> <gloss>great ancestral sacrifice</gloss> sacrifice. When sacrificing to the various dukes, they are paired with <term>Wen Wang</term> <gloss>King Wen of Zhou</gloss> and sacrificed to in the Zhou temple. A detailed investigation shows that sacrifices in the Ancestral Temple are also called <term>Di</term>. When sacrificing to the various dukes, they are paired with King Wen and sacrificed to in the Zhou temple. Master Zhu <note>Zhu Xi</note> states that ancient rituals have been completely lost and cannot be fully investigated. The Great <term>Xia</term> <gloss>collective ancestral sacrifice</gloss> sacrifice is used to replace the <term>Di</term> sacrifice. In the 8th year of Duke Zhuang, there was a sacrifice in the Zhou temple, and Duke Xi necessarily paired it with the Zhou temple. Why did he not do this in the Great Temple <note>the temple of the founding ancestor of the State of Lu</note>? Because Duke Xi had his own years and numbers <note>his own place in the generational order</note> which all combined to make it so.

The scholar Zheng Kangcheng <note>Zheng Xuan</note> cited the events of the 8th year to prove that the State of Lu had a Zhou temple, saying that they retroactively included King Wen. Regarding the 8th year of Duke Xi and the events of Duke Xuan, when the mourning period was completed, a <term>Di</term> sacrifice was held in the Great Temple. Every three years there is one <term>Di</term> sacrifice. Therefore, in the 2nd year of Duke Xi, there was a Great <term>Di</term> in the Great Temple, which refers to the 2nd year of Duke Min <note>referring to the transition of the tablet</note>. Because the mourning for Duke Min was finished, his tablet was moved to the ancestral temple and sacrificed to. This is called the <term>Xia</term> sacrifice.

Furthermore, Zheng Kangcheng cited the Son of Heaven and the Feudal Lords, saying that after the mourning period is over, the <term>Xia</term> is held, followed by the <term>Di</term>. This follows the commentary of Master Zuo <note>Zuo Qiuming</note>. Since the <term>Xia</term> is a collective sacrifice, the <term>Di</term> is used as a replacement. Thus, everything follows the Great Temple, where they collectively partake in the sacrificial offerings.

As for the State of Lu, they possessed the Zhou Temple to retroactively honor King Wen, and they paired him with the Duke of Zhou <note>the first lord of Lu</note>. The various ancestral tablets could not be shifted from their constant positions. It is said that Duke Zhuang clearly used the ritual objects of the Son of Heaven. Not only did he retroactively honor King Wen, but he also paired him with the Duke of Zhou. Mr. Zhao <note>Zhao Pengfei</note> stated that Duke Zhuang did not retroactively pair them, therefore the text says Duke Zhuang committed an act of arrogance in his own temple. By practicing these rituals, he did not retroactively pair the ancestors.

Furthermore, Mr. Zhao, known as Boxun, said: The fact that Lu did not use the <term>Di</term> sacrifice was because it belonged to the Temple of the Duke of Zhou and reached up to King Wen. How can one be certain that the <term>Di</term> sacrifice of Duke Min for Duke Zhuang necessarily involved a retroactive pairing, and further, that it necessarily involved a collective offering?

<column-break/>
It is also called <term>Di</term>, and the <term>Di</term>... <meta>continues to the next page: ...sacrifice is the most important.</meta>

Regarding the sacrifice at the Ancestral Temple: The sacrifice at the temple of the Duke of Zhou is the ancestral sacrifice. Regarding the *Di* <gloss>a specific major ancestral sacrifice</gloss> at the temple of the Duke of Zhuang: Duke Zhuang of Lu usurped the rites by performing the *Di* sacrifice in his own temple. This is why the scholars say he did not use the correct ritual objects. The *Di* sacrifice is not for the purpose of posthumously honoring a distant ancestor; it is to match them with the Duke of Zhou. Regarding Duke Min: The *Di* sacrifice at his temple is called the *Di* sacrifice. It was performed at the Great Ancestral Temple in the second year following the completion of the mourning period for Duke Zhuang. This is the origin of the *Di* sacrifice in the Great Ancestral Temple. The ancient rites were largely lost, and the Zhao clan states that the *Di* sacrifice of Duke Zhuang should not have been performed. Duke Min followed the Duke of Zhou. His rituals were the ancestral ones of the Zhou Temple. The *Jia* <gloss>a combined ancestral sacrifice</gloss> is performed every three years. The *Di* sacrifice is performed every eight years. The *Zuo Zhuan* <gloss>Commentary of Zuo</gloss> records the rituals of the feudal lords. Duke Xi and Duke Xuan of Lu followed these rules. The *Di* sacrifice at the ancestral temple was based on the eight-year cycle. This serves as evidence of the ritual system of the state of Lu.

<summary>This passage discusses the ritual improprieties committed by Duke Zhuang of Lu regarding the Di sacrifice and clarifies the correct performance of ancestral rites in the state of Lu relative to the temple of the Duke of Zhou.</summary>
<keywords>Di sacrifice, Jia sacrifice, Duke Zhuang, Duke Min, Lu, Ancestral Temple, ritual propriety</keywords>
