Imperial Collection of Four Treasuries

<margin>Imperial Collection of Four Treasuries</margin>
<margin>Summary</margin>

The work is organized into fourteen categories, including Sincerity and Rectification, Cultivation and Regulation, Governance and Pacification, the Way of Heaven, the Way of Man, the various Confucian scholars, unorthodox schools of thought, and the Classics, Philosophers, Histories, and Compendia. The scholarship of Lu Shiyi <note>the author</note> focuses on the importance of maintaining respect for ritual and law, rather than empty discourse. His principles regarding sincerity and reverence emphasize the implementation of practical governance, rather than idle focus on the internal study of nature and mind. Among modern scholars, his work is considered the most reliable and grounded.

He stated: "When there are no people in the world discussing learning, the state of the world is in decline; yet when everyone in the world is discussing learning, that is also a sign of the world's decline." During the Jiajing and Longqing reigns <note>mid-to-late 16th century</note>, academies were established everywhere. People gathered in groups, often by the thousands, merely following shadows and chasing echoes, wasting time and neglecting their duties, with some even using these assemblies to pursue private interests. This is what is known as the reckless criticism of self-proclaimed hermits. He also said: "What we should be learning today..."

<summary>This passage provides an editorial summary of Lu Shiyi’s scholarship, emphasizing his preference for practical governance and ritual over speculative philosophy, and his critique of the performative intellectual culture prevalent in the Ming dynasty academies.</summary>
<keywords>Lu Shiyi, Ming dynasty, Confucianism, academies, practical governance, ritual, intellectual history</keywords>

# Imperial Sanctioned Complete Library of the Four Treasuries
## Abstract

<margin>Imperial Sanctioned Complete Library of the Four Treasuries</margin>
<margin>Abstract</margin>

The work covers fourteen categories: Sincerity and Rectification <note>referring to the cultivation of the mind and intention</note>, Cultivation and Regulation <note>of the self and the family</note>, Governance and Peace <note>of the state and the world</note>, the Way of Heaven, the Way of Humanity, Various Scholars, Heterodox Schools, and the Classics, Philosophers, and Histories. The scholarship of <term>Shiyi</term> <gloss>Lu Shiyi, 1611 to 1672</gloss> is centered on the reverent observance of ritual law rather than empty talk on the principles of sincerity and reverence. His focus is on the implementation of practical governance rather than the hollow practice of investigating the nature of the mind. Among recent schools of lecturers, his work is considered the most sincere and substantial. Therefore, he says: When there are no people in the world who discuss learning, this marks the decline of the moral Way; yet when everyone in the world is discussing learning, this also marks the decline of the moral Way. During the <term>Jia-Long</term> <gloss>the reigns of the Jiajing and Longqing Emperors, 1522 to 1572</gloss> periods, academies spread throughout the empire, gathering friends and attracting followers by the thousands. They chased shadows and echoed sounds, wasting time and neglecting affairs. Some even used these gatherings to pursue private interests. This is what is called the "unbridled arguments of scholars in retirement" <note>referring to intellectuals who hold no office but criticize the government</note>. He also says: What should be studied today...

<summary>This abstract evaluates the scholarly approach of Lu Shiyi, emphasizing his preference for practical governance and ritual over the empty philosophical debates common in the late Ming dynasty. It criticizes the excessive growth of private academies and the superficiality of contemporary intellectual culture.</summary>

On that day, the director led the artisans into the residence. The Imperial Musician <term>Xielü Lang</term> <gloss>Assistant Director of Music</gloss> raised the banner, and the music began. When he lowered the banner, the music stopped. The civil dances withdrew, and the military dances advanced; this was the usual system. During the An Lushan Rebellion <term>Tianbao Zhi Luan</term>, Emperor Suzong recovered the two capitals <term>Liangjing</term>. From the Zhìdé <gloss>era name</gloss> onwards, only on New Year's Day, when receiving felicitations at Hanyuan Hall <term>Hanyuan Dian</term>, were palace musical frames <term>Gongjia</term> set up. For all other suburban sacrifices and major temple rites, there was only <term>dengge</term> <gloss>ascending music for the altar</gloss>, with no music or dance in the courtyard below the altar. After Emperor Xizong's Guangming era <term>Guangming Zhi Hou</term>, court music <term>jinzou</term> was almost lost, and among those sought out to build the frames and instruments, hardly any remained. When Emperor Zhaozong was about to visit the suburban temples, the relevant officials requested the creation of framed music. Thereupon, the Chancellor Zhang Jun was appointed as the Commissioner for Repairing and Constructing Instruments and Frames. He gathered all the artisans from the Imperial Sacrificial Court <term>Taichang</term> and questioned them, but they could not find the correct methods. Doctor Shang Yingsun, who was skilled in ancient practices, used the stands for bells and stone chimes <term>sunju</term> as a model to cast bells, adjusting their weight and pitch. He then reset the arranged bells <term>bianzhong</term> to match and correct them, establishing the <term>Huangzhong</term> <gloss>Yellow Bell</gloss> at nine inches and five fen, which is double the <term>Yingzhong</term> <gloss>Responding Bell</gloss>.

# Cloud Dragon
According to the *History of Yuan, Treatise on Carriages and Attire*, the Grand General of the Imperial Guard, holding two large yellow dragon banners with images, was attended by two banner-bearers, eight attendants, and eleven riders in brocade hats and colorful scarves, each with a vibrant color.

# Robes
### Red Silk with Gold Embroidery
In the *Dreams of Splendor of the Eastern Capital*, when a princess was married, ceremonial guards, moving curtains, and screen walls were arranged. Dozens of palace maids, all adorned with pearl hairpins, hanging ornaments, and intricate clustered silk headdresses, rode horses wearing robes and capes, with double reins and double wraps, led by a blue canopy.

# Ocher Yellow Brocade
In the *History of Tang, Treatise on Carriages and Attire*, Emperor Wen of Sui's court attire was an ocher yellow brocade robe, worn with a black gauze hat and a folded headscarf.

# Five-Color Embroidered Silk
In the *History of Song, Treatise on Music*, the system for troupe dances included the "Zhezhi Dance Troupe," whose members wore five-color embroidered silk robes and <unclear>six-harmony shoes</unclear>, which were also worn by high officials.

# Inscribed with Palindromic Phrases
In the *History of Tang, Treatise on Carriages and Attire*, when Empress Wu monopolized power, she often bestowed embroidered robes and headscarves on her officials, some of which were inscribed with palindromic phrases. These garments, generally wide robes, lacked proper regulations and are not worth detailing.

# Colors Favored Blue-Green
In the *History of Southern Dynasties, Biography of Hou Jing*, there was a children's rhyme in the Datong period: "Blue silk and white horse, from Shouyang he comes." When Hou Jing was defeated at Yang, he requested brocade, but the court provided blue cloth. Later, all his robes were made of this blue cloth. Hou Jing rode a white horse with blue silk reins, intending to fulfill the rhyme.

# Spring Grass as a Robe
Bai Juyi's poem "Autumn frost is like a beard, years grow long in vain, a position is still early." Also, Li Shangyin's "Spring Excursion" poem says, "Master Yu is the youngest, green grass envies his spring robe." Wen Tingyun's letter states, "After anointing with oil, disheveled hair becomes the temples, and after the last bit of silver and gold, green grass becomes the robe."

## Note: The four metal instruments are all used for military training and hunting. In military affairs, the drums are used first, and then the metal instruments. This pertains to the duties of the Great Minister of War <note>original: "Da Sima"</note>.

<column-break/>

They harmonize with the drums. The **zhuo** <gloss>a small bell-shaped instrument</gloss> is a **zheng** <gloss>a gong or bell used for signaling</gloss>. Its shape is like a small bell. <margin>Master Ma Duanlin says: The Book of Odes mentions "the gong-men strike the drums," and the State Discourses <note>original: "Guoyu"</note> mentions the "ding-ning" signal.</margin>
Its sound is heavy. From the perspective of its specific sound, it is called a **zhuo**; from the perspective of its use in alerting people, it is called a **zheng**. In reality, they are the same thing. **It is sounded when the army is on the march.** <gloss>From the perspective of correcting or directing people, it is called a zheng, but they are one instrument.</gloss>
**It is used to provide the rhythm for the drums.** Regarding the duties of the Minister of War: the **zhuo** is sounded when the army marches. <gloss>Jia's Commentary <note>original: "Jia Shu"</note> says: This refers to the Duke's army.</gloss> The **nao** <gloss>a small hand-bell</gloss> is like a bell but has no clapper. It has a handle to hold and sound it, used to stop the beating of the drums. Regarding the duties of the Minister of War: sound the **nao** to signal a retreat. <gloss>Jia's Commentary says: When the army advances</gloss> the drums are beaten; when they retreat, the **nao** is used. The **duo** <gloss>a large hand-bell</gloss> is a large bell. It is shaken to communicate with the drums. Regarding the duties of the Minister of War: the Minister of War shakes the **duo**. <gloss>Jia's Commentary says: This is a metal bell with a metal clapper, so it is called a metal duo. Those shaken in the military are metal bells; those with wooden clappers are wooden duo, which are shaken when issuing commands.</gloss> The local military officers <note>original: "Liang Sima"</note> shake the **duo**. When the army generals and those below them hear it, they strike the drums, which is why it is said to "communicate with the drums."

<summary>This page describes the four metal percussion instruments used in ancient Chinese military maneuvers to signal movements and coordinate with drums. It identifies the zhuo, zheng, nao, and duo, explaining their physical forms and specific ritual functions in advancing or retreating.</summary>
<keywords>Rites of Zhou, military music, percussion instruments, Minister of War, signaling, drumming, ancient warfare rituals</keywords>

## Note: The four types of metal instruments are all used for military expeditions and hunting. In military matters, the drum comes first, followed by the metal instruments. This is according to the duties of the Grand Marshal (<term>Da Sima</term>).

<column-break/>

They harmonize with the drums. 

**The <term>Zhuo</term>**: This is the <term>Zheng</term> <gloss>gong-like percussion instrument</gloss>. Its shape is like a small bell. <note>Ma Duanlin says: In the Book of Odes, it is written "the gong-men strike the drums," in the states this is called the <term>Zheng</term>.</note> Its sound is deep. When speaking of it in terms of alerting people, it is called <term>Zhuo</term>; when speaking of it in terms of keeping them in order, it is called <term>Zheng</term>. They are, in fact, the same. 

**Sounded during military marches.** <note>To enjoin and warn, when speaking of it in terms of correcting people, it is called <term>Zheng</term>; they are in fact the same.</note> 

**Used to set the rhythm for the drums.** According to the duties of the Marshal: when the army marches, sound the <term>Zhuo</term>. <note>Jia's Commentary says: That refers to the public.</note> 

**The <term>Nao</term>**: Like a bell, but without a tongue. It has a handle to hold and sound it, used to stop the beating of the drums. According to the duties of the Marshal: sound the <term>Nao</term> to retreat. <note>Jia's Commentary says: When advancing the army, beat the drums; to retreat...</note> 

**The <term>Duo</term>**: A large bell. It is shaken to signal the drums. According to the duties of the Marshal: the Marshal shakes the <term>Duo</term>. <note>Jia's Commentary says: This is a metal bell with a metal tongue, hence it is called a metal <term>Duo</term>. Those in the army that are shaken with a metal bell and a metal tongue are the metal <term>Duo</term>, which are shaken when orders are issued. The two Marshals shake the <term>Duo</term>. Below the level of the army generals, they then beat the drums; hence it is said to signal the drums.</note>

<summary>This page explains the functions of four specific metal percussion instruments—the Zhuo, Zheng, Nao, and Duo—within the military ritual system described in the Rites of Zhou.</summary>
<keywords>Rites of Zhou, military ritual, percussion instruments, Da Sima, Jia Gongyan, Ma Duanlin</keywords>

# The Guoyu on the Establishment of the Pitch Standard

## To Determine Measurements: The Ancient Blind Musicians Evaluated the Central Pitch, Measured it, and Created the System of Pitch Standards and Bell Calibration

### Using the Central Pitch to Determine the Pitch Standard, and Using the Pitch Standard to Establish the Calibration of the Bells

The <term>Jia Shu</term> <gloss>The Commentary by Jia Gongyan</gloss> cites the <term>Guoyu</term> <gloss>Discourses of the States</gloss> to explain that in determining the size [of the pipes], one must ensure they correspond to the pitch standards. The "central pitch" refers to the generation of the upper and lower notes, which determines the length of the pitch pipes. "Measuring the pitch standard" refers to calculating by the pipes. Establishing the calibration of the bells based on doubling or halving [the pipe length] is what determines the length of the corresponding pitch pipes. Regarding this: examining the original meaning of the <term>Guoyu</term>, it means examining the central pitch to create the <term>Huangzhong</term> pipe. "Measuring it" refers to carefully inspecting the consistency of the central pitch. "Measuring the pitch standard" means that once the dimensions of the <term>Huangzhong</term> are obtained, one then measures the fractions of the upper and lower generations to determine the short and long dimensions of the twelve pitch pipes. "Calibrating the bells" refers to establishing the standard calibration based on the pitch pipes, in order to tune the sounds of the twelve pitch pipes and the bells.

# The Discourses of the States: The pitches are that by which the standard scales are established.

## They emerge from measurement. The spirit-blind musicians of antiquity examined the middle tones and measured them with standardized systems to regulate the pitches and the tuning of the bells.

### Using the middle tones to fix the pitches, and using the pitches to establish the standard scale for the bells.

Jia’s Commentary <note>referring to the scholar Jia Gongyan</note> cites the Discourses of the States <note>original: "Guoyu"</note> because he wishes to show that the size of the instruments must correspond to the pitches. "Middle tones" refers to the upward and downward generation that determines the length of the pitch pipes. "Measuring the pitches" means calculating the pitches based on the standard pipes, using the principle of doubling or halving the length to establish the scale of the bells. This ensures they correspond to the length of the pitch pipes. According to the original meaning of the Discourses of the States, "examining the middle tones" refers to creating the Yellow Bell pipe. "Measuring them" means carefully observing the standard measure of the middle tones. "Measuring the pitches" means that once the dimensions of the Yellow Bell are obtained, one calculates the fractions for upward and downward generation to determine the lengths of the twelve pitch pipes. "Tuning the bells" means establishing the scale based on the pitch pipes to harmonize the sounds of the twelve pitches and the two types of bells.

The tradition states: The Rong were about to invade Cao. Cao Ji remonstrated, saying: "The Rong are numerous and act without righteousness. My lord, I request that you do not oppose them yourself." The Earl of Cao would not listen. After being remonstrated with three times without success, Cao Ji left. He Xiu says: There are five types of remonstrance. The first is "allusive remonstrance," as practiced by Confucius. <note>Note: Regarding the twelfth year of Duke Ding, the Gongyang Commentary states: Confucius, hearing of the Ji clan's actions, requested an audience with Ji Sun and said: "A noble house should not store armaments, and a walled city should not exceed one hundred zhi <gloss>a unit of measurement for city walls</gloss>; you should dismantle the Fei city."</note> The second is "compliant remonstrance," as practiced by Cao Ji. <note>Note: This refers to the aforementioned remonstrance to the ruler of Cao.</note> The third is "straightforward remonstrance," as practiced by Zi Jiaju. <note>Note: Regarding the twenty-fifth year of Duke Zhao, the Gongyang Commentary states: The Duke of Zhao had long usurped the rituals of the Son of Heaven, and the high ministers had long usurped those of the feudal lords. This is to speak plainly about the ruler's usurpation without evasion.</note> The fourth is "argumentative remonstrance," as practiced by Zi Fan when he requested to withdraw. <note>Note: Regarding the fifteenth year of Duke Xuan, the Gongyang Commentary states: King Zhuang of Chu besieged Song. Song's Zi Fan and Hua Yuan rode on mounds <gloss>earthen platforms used for observing the enemy or shooting arrows</gloss> and spoke to each other. Hua Yuan said to Zi Fan: "We are exchanging our children to eat them and splitting their bones to cook them." Zi Fan said to Hua Yuan: "Our army has seven days of provisions left." Zi Fan urged the King of Chu to retreat.</note> The fifth is "blunt remonstrance." <note>Note: He pardoned Song and returned. After repeated remonstrance went unheeded, he led his troops away, and the King of Chu also returned.</note>

<summary>This text classifies five methods of moral remonstrance according to the Gongyang Commentary, using historical examples from the Spring and Autumn period to demonstrate appropriate strategies for advising a ruler.</summary>
<keywords>remonstrance, Gongyang Commentary, He Xiu, political ethics, Spring and Autumn period, Cao Ji, Confucius, usurpation</keywords>
translations.T2:
The Commentary says: The <term>Rong</term> <gloss>non-Chinese tribes of the west</gloss> were about to invade <term>Cao</term> <gloss>a small state in the Spring and Autumn period</gloss>. <term>Cao Ji</term> <gloss>an official of the state of Cao</gloss> advised his ruler, saying, "The Rong are numerous and act without righteousness; I request that my Lord does not face them personally." The Earl of Cao would not listen. After advising him three times and being ignored, <term>Cao Ji</term> then left him. <term>He Xiu</term> <gloss>a prominent Han dynasty commentator on the Gongyang Zhuan</gloss> says there are five types of remonstrance.

The first is called <term>Feng Jian</term> <gloss>persuasive or satirical remonstrance</gloss>. Confucius was such a man. <gloss>Note: The Gongyang Commentary for the twelfth year of Duke Ding says that Confucius, having heard of the Ji family's power, told Ji Sun that families should not store armor and cities should not have walls over one hundred measures in height. This led to the dismantling of the walls of Fei city.</gloss>

The second is called <term>Shun Jian</term> <gloss>compliant or indirect remonstrance</gloss>. <term>Cao Ji</term> was such a man. <gloss>Note: This refers to the advice given to the Earl of Cao mentioned above.</gloss>

The third is called <term>Zhi Jian</term> <gloss>direct or upright remonstrance</gloss>. <term>Zijia Ju</term> <gloss>an official of the state of Lu</gloss> was such a man. <gloss>Note: The Gongyang Commentary for the twenty-fifth year of Duke Zhao says that Duke Zhao acted toward the Son of Heaven as the Great Officers acted toward the feudal lords. He had usurped status for a long time. Zijia Ju spoke of this without avoiding the topic of the ruler's usurpation.</gloss>

The fourth is called <term>Zheng Jian</term> <gloss>argumentative remonstrance</gloss>. <term>Zifan</term> <gloss>a general of the state of Chu</gloss> requesting to return home was such an instance. <gloss>Note: The Gongyang Commentary for the fifteenth year of Duke Xuan says that King Zhuang of Chu besieged Song. Zifan and Hua Yuan of Song spoke to each other while standing on the siege mounds. Hua Yuan told Zifan that the people of Song were swapping their children to eat them and splitting human bones for firewood. Zifan told Hua Yuan that the Chu army only had seven days of rations left. Zifan then urged the King of Chu to return home.</gloss>

The fifth is called <term>Gang Jian</term> <gloss>stubborn or blunt remonstrance</gloss>. <gloss>Note: This refers to when an official repeatedly advises against a course of action, and when not heard, leads the army away. In the case of Zifan, after the King of Chu pardoned Song and returned, Zifan had repeatedly advised him. When not heard, he led the army away from Chu, and the King eventually followed.</gloss>

<summary>This page discusses the five categories of remonstrance defined by the commentator He Xiu, illustrated with historical examples from the Spring and Autumn period. It defines different ways an official may advise a ruler, ranging from subtle persuasion to direct confrontation.</summary>
<keywords>remonstrance, He Xiu, Cao Ji, Confucius, Gongyang Zhuan, political ethics, Spring and Autumn period, state of Cao, state of Chu</keywords>

The spirit drum, the spirit thunder-drum, the flutes of Sunzhu, the qin and se of Kongsang, and the dance of Xianchi. On the summer solstice, perform them on the square mound in the marsh. If the music transforms eight times, then all earthly spirits will emerge, and one can pay them reverence.

<margin>Commentary on the Classic of Music</margin>

<note>A description of the musical instruments and ritual procedures for the winter solstice ceremony:</note> Using the <term>gu</term> <gloss>large drum</gloss>, <term>tao</term> <gloss>small pellet-drum</gloss>, the pipes made of <term>guzhu</term> <gloss>bamboo from the lone bamboo region</gloss>, and the <term>yunhe</term> <gloss>cloud-harmonizing</gloss> zithers and lutes, perform the dance of <term>yunmen</term> <gloss>Cloud Gate</gloss> at the circular mound on the ground during the winter solstice. When this music is played and reaches its sixth transformation, the heavenly spirits will all descend, and one may then perform the rites for them. In all such music, the <term>hanzhong</term> <gloss>bell of the harmonious sphere</gloss> serves as the <term>gong</term> <gloss>tonic note</gloss>, <term>dacu</term> <gloss>the major cluster</gloss> as the <term>jue</term> <gloss>third note</gloss>, <term>guxi</term> <gloss>the ancient wash</gloss> as the <term>zhi</term> <gloss>fifth note</gloss>, and <term>nanlü</term> <gloss>the southern pitch</gloss> as the <term>yu</term> <gloss>sixth note</gloss>.

<note>A description of the musical instruments and ritual procedures for the summer solstice ceremony:</note> Using the <term>linggu</term> <gloss>spirit drum</gloss>, <term>lingtao</term> <gloss>spirit pellet-drum</gloss>, the pipes of <term>sunzhu</term> <gloss>bamboo of the grandson</gloss>, and the <term>kongsang</term> <gloss>empty mulberry</gloss> zithers and lutes, perform the dance of <term>xianchi</term> <gloss>the pond of universal harmony</gloss> at the square mound in the marsh during the summer solstice. When this music is played and reaches its eighth transformation, the earthly deities will all emerge, and one may then perform the rites for them. In all such music, the <term>huangzhong</term> <gloss>yellow bell</gloss> <note>Should be read as <term>yuanzhong</term> <gloss>round bell</gloss></note> serves as the <term>gong</term> <gloss>tonic note</gloss>, <term>dalu</term> <gloss>the grand pitch</gloss> <note>Should be read as <term>dalu</term> <gloss>grand pitch</gloss></note> as the <term>jue</term> <gloss>third note</gloss>, <term>dacu</term> <gloss>the major cluster</gloss> as the <term>zhi</term> <gloss>fifth note</gloss>, and <term>yingzhong</term> <gloss>the resonant bell</gloss> as the <term>yu</term> <gloss>sixth note</gloss>.

Using the <term>lugu</term> <gloss>road drum</gloss>, <term>lutao</term> <gloss>road pellet-drum</gloss>, the pipes of <term>yinzhu</term> <gloss>yin bamboo</gloss>, and the <term>longmen</term> <gloss>dragon gate</gloss> zithers and lutes, perform the songs of <term>jiude</term> <gloss>nine virtues</gloss> and the dances of <term>jiuqing</term> <gloss>nine stone chimes</gloss> within the ancestral temple. When this music is played and reaches its ninth transformation, the spirits of the ancestors may then be worshipped through these rites.

<summary>This page details the specific instruments, musical scales, and ritual transformations required for ceremonies held at the circular mound, square mound, and ancestral temple to commune with heavenly, earthly, and ancestral spirits.</summary>
<keywords>Music, Ritual, Solstice, Ancestral Temple, Instruments, Spirits, Tuning, Ceremonial Dance</keywords>

When this music is performed in its six variations, the heavenly spirits all descend, and it becomes possible to perform the rites for them. In all such music, the <term>Hanzhong</term> <gloss>Forest Bell</gloss> pitch is the <term>Gong</term> <gloss>the first note of the pentatonic scale</gloss>, <term>Taicu</term> <gloss>Great Framework</gloss> is the <term>Jue</term> <gloss>third note</gloss>, <term>Guxi</term> <gloss>Old Purified</gloss> is the <term>Zhi</term> <gloss>fourth note</gloss>, and <term>Nanlü</term> <gloss>Southern Law</gloss> is the <term>Yu</term> <gloss>fifth note</gloss>.

The Spirit Drum <note>original: 靈鼓; a drum with six faces used for earthly sacrifices</note>, the Spirit Hand-drum <note>original: 靈鼗</note>, flutes made of bamboo shoots <note>original: 孫竹; young bamboo from the roots of the parent plant</note>, the lutes of Kongsang <note>original: 空桑; Hollow Mulberry mountain</note>, and the Dance of the Jade Pond <note>original: 咸池</note> are used at the summer solstice on the Square Mound <gloss>the altar of Earth</gloss> in the midst of the marshes. When this music is performed in its eight variations, the earthly spirits all emerge, and it becomes possible to perform the rites for them. 

In all such music, <term>Huangzhong</term> <gloss>Yellow Bell</gloss> <margin>should be read as Yuanzhong <gloss>Harmonious Bell</gloss></margin> is the <term>Gong</term> <gloss>first note</gloss> <margin>should be read as Dalü <gloss>Great Law</gloss></margin>, <term>Dalü</term> <gloss>Great Law</gloss> is the <term>Jue</term> <gloss>third note</gloss>, <term>Taicu</term> <gloss>Great Framework</gloss> is the <term>Zhi</term> <gloss>fourth note</gloss>, and <term>Yingzhong</term> <gloss>Answering Bell</gloss> is the <term>Yu</term> <gloss>fifth note</gloss>. The Royal Drum <note>original: 路鼓; a drum with four faces used for ancestral rites</note>, the Royal Hand-drum <note>original: 路鼗</note>, flutes made of bamboo from the shaded valley <note>original: 陰竹</note>, the lutes of Longmen <note>original: 龍門; Dragon Gate mountain</note>, the Songs of the Nine Virtues, and the Dance of the Nine Chimes are used within the Ancestral Temple. The Proclamation Officers and others separately lead the civil and military officials who are performing the ceremony or assisting in the sacrificial rites. These officials, having carefully fastened their jade pendants, enter the courtyard of the Daqing Palace <note>The Palace of Great Celebration, the main hall for state ceremonies</note> to stand in their ranks. The Ceremonial Officers and Proclamation Officers lead the Vice Minister of the Ministry of Rites to memorialize the request for "internal readiness" <note>a signal that the Emperor is preparing to emerge</note>. After a short while, he again memorializes "external readiness" <note>a signal that all preparations outside are complete</note>. The Keepers of the Imperial Seals present the seals and arrange them to the left and right of the imperial couch. He rides in the imperial carriage while the clearing of the path and the imperial shouts are announced. The guards and attendants follow the standard protocol. He travels from the west chamber to the west side of the imperial couch and descends from the carriage. The Emperor then takes his seat on the imperial throne facing south. The attending ministers stand on both sides. The Ushers of the Palace Gate Bureau, positioned before the couch, call out the commands for the Bureau of Military Affairs to perform the ritual bows.

# Volume 40

### Ritual Offerings of Wine and Spirits

For the primary and associated deity positions, the <term>taizun</term> <gloss>great vessel</gloss> is filled with <term>fanqi</term> <gloss>floating wine</gloss> and <term>liqi</term> <gloss>sweet wine</gloss>. The <term>zhuzun</term> <gloss>manifest vessel</gloss> is filled with <term>angqi</term> <gloss>bubbling wine</gloss>. The <term>xizun</term> <gloss>sacrificial ox vessel</gloss> is filled with <term>tiqi</term> <gloss>reddish wine</gloss>. The <term>shanlei</term> <gloss>mountain-patterned jar</gloss> is filled with <term>xijiu</term> <gloss>aged wine</gloss>. These are placed atop the altar.

The <term>taizun</term> <gloss>great vessel</gloss> is also filled with <term>shenqi</term> <gloss>sunken wine</gloss>. The <term>shanlei</term> <gloss>mountain jars</gloss> are filled with <term>shijiu</term> <gloss>service wine</gloss> and <term>qingjiu</term> <gloss>clear wine</gloss>. These are placed below the altar.

For the subordinate sacrificial positions, the <term>zhuzun</term> <gloss>manifest vessel</gloss> is filled with <term>liqi</term> <gloss>sweet wine</gloss> and <term>angqi</term> <gloss>bubbling wine</gloss>. The <term>xizun</term> <gloss>sacrificial ox vessel</gloss> is filled with <term>shijiu</term> <gloss>service wine</gloss>.

### Grain Offerings

For both the primary and associated positions as well as the subordinate sacrifices, the <term>fu</term> <gloss>rectangular grain vessels</gloss> are filled with broomcorn millet and foxtail millet. The <term>gui</term> <gloss>round grain vessels</gloss> are filled with rice and spiked millet.

### Contents of the Ritual Baskets and Bowls

For the primary and associated positions at the <term>Fangqiu</term> <gloss>Square Mound, the Altar to Earth</gloss>, each <term>bian</term> <gloss>bamboo basket</gloss> is filled respectively with: dried salt, dried fish, dates, chestnuts, hazelnuts, water caltrops, foxnuts, dried venison, black rice cakes, white rice cakes, parched grain cakes, and bean flour cakes.

Each <term>dou</term> <gloss>wooden bowl</gloss> is filled respectively with: pickled leeks, minced meat in brine, pickled greens, minced venison, pickled celery, minced rabbit, pickled bamboo shoots, minced fish, pickled tripe, minced pork, <term>baoshi</term> <gloss>finished food vegetable stew</gloss>, and <term>sanshi</term> <gloss>grain and meat paste</gloss>.

For the subordinate sacrifices, the contents of the <term>bian</term> <gloss>bamboo baskets</gloss> exclude the parched grain cakes and bean flour cakes. The <term>dou</term> <gloss>wooden bowls</gloss> exclude the vegetable stew and the grain and meat paste.

### Ceremonial Settings

The placement of the seating mats uses crimson fabric, following the same protocol as the <term>Jiaotian</term> <gloss>Sacrifice to Heaven at the Suburban Altar</gloss>. The chariots and banners used are also the same as those used for the sacrifice to Heaven.

<summary>This page details the specific types of ritual wines, grains, and prepared foods required for ceremonies at the Square Mound Altar to Earth. It specifies which vessels are used for primary versus subordinate deities and notes that the ceremonial mats and banners mirror those used in the Sacrifice to Heaven.</summary>
<keywords>Square Mound, Altar to Earth, ritual vessels, sacrificial wine, grain offerings, food offerings, Qing dynasty ritual, ritual protocol</keywords>

That this differs from the music name in the current classic's commentary is because the Yellow Emperor's original music was named <term>Xianchi</term>. Because the Duke of Zhou kept the Yellow Emperor’s <term>Xianchi</term> as the name for Yao's music, he established the name <term>Yunmen</term> <gloss>Cloud Gate</gloss> for the Yellow Emperor's music, equating it with the <term>Dajuan</term>. Originally, the Yellow Emperor’s music was called the Salt Pond. Because the Five Emperors lived in different times, they did not necessarily follow the same musical traditions. If Emperor Yao expanded and refined the structure of the Yellow Emperor's music while keeping its original name, it remained the Salt Pond, which is the Great Salt mentioned here. If the musical structure remained as it was without expansion, the original name was changed and called the Great Brilliance. Thus, it is said that the Great Brilliance is the music of Emperor Yao. When the Duke of Zhou composed music, he further created the Grand Scroll. The Grand Scroll is the same as the Great Brilliance. Although the Great Brilliance is the name for Emperor Yao's music, its structure is derived from the Yellow Emperor's music; therefore, this Grand Scroll is also considered the music of the Yellow Emperor. Since the Duke of Zhou considered that the Yellow Emperor's Salt Pond was used as the name for Yao's music, he established another name for the Yellow Emperor's music called the Cloud Gate <note>original: "Yunmen" 雲門</note>. Because the Cloud Gate and the Grand Scroll are considered as one, in the following text where music is categorized and ordered, the Grand Scroll is not listed separately. In the sixth year of Emperor Gaozu of Han, it was renamed the Literary Beginning and Five Elements Dance.</gloss> Based on this, we know there was a tradition of changing the names of musical works. According to the Apocrypha of the Classic of Filial Piety <note>original: "Xiaojing wei" 孝經緯</note>, the music of Fuxi was called Establishing the Foundation <note>original: "Liji" 立基</note>, the music of Shennong was called Consulting the Humble <note>original: "Xiamou" 下謀</note>, and the music of Zhurong was called Connected Succession <note>original: "Shuxu" 屬續</note>.

作柷夏者也云笙師教之則三器在庭
可知其在庭可知
笙管在堂下近堂則三者亦在
堂下遠堂在庭可知云

至之時吹之冬水用事水數六六七四十二竽之長蓋

在左方竽象三十六管宮管在中央禮圖云竽長四
尺二寸此竽三十六簧與禮圖同云篪七空者廣雅云
篪以竹為之長尺四寸八孔一孔上出寸三分禮圖云
篪九空司農云七孔蓋寫者誤當云八空也或司農別
有所見云春牘以竹大五六寸長七尺短者一二尺其

<meta>This page continues the technical description of ritual musical instruments from the Rites of Zhou, specifically detailing their dimensions, materials, and symbolic significance according to various classical commentaries.</meta>

The <term>yu</term> <gloss>tiger-shaped scraper</gloss> is shaped like a lacquered tube with a narrowed mouth, measuring two <term>wei</term> <gloss>girths</gloss> in circumference and five feet six inches in length. It is covered with sheepskin leather and has two handle-loops. The <term>shu-hua</term> <gloss>sparse decorative paintings</gloss> on it are understood by reference to the laws of the Han dynasty. <term>Zheng Xuan</term> <note>a prominent Han dynasty commentator</note> notes in the section on the <term>jin-che</term> <gloss>Official of the Carriage</gloss> that the <term>zhu</term> <gloss>wooden percussion box</gloss> is colored with much red and little black. Regarding the <term>shu-hua</term>, it refers to drawing long, spaced-out patterns. <term>Zheng Zichun</term> <note>an earlier Han scholar</note> reads the word for "distant" as <term>di</term> <gloss>to cleanse or wash</gloss>. He follows the reading from the <term>Jiao Te Sheng</term> <gloss>The Single Victim at the Border Sacrifice</gloss> section of the Book of Rites, which describes the state where "the odors and flavors are not yet fully formed, yet all is pure and cleansed," referring to the sound being "cleansed." He says this refers to the five-holed bamboo flute blown in modern times. <term>Zheng Xuan</term> later followed this interpretation. It is said that the <term>zhu</term> music is the music of the Xia dynasty because the <term>zhong-shi</term> <gloss>Master of Bells</gloss> oversees the <term>zhu</term> music. Since this <term>zhu</term> music is the same, we know that the <term>zhu</term> music taught here is the Xia dynasty music created by the Master of Bells. It says the <term>sheng-shi</term> <gloss>Master of Reed Pipes</gloss> teaches it; thus it can be known that these three instruments are located in the courtyard. If the <term>sheng</term> <gloss>small reed pipe</gloss> and <term>guan</term> <gloss>double-reed pipe</gloss> are below the hall and near the hall, then these three are also below the hall, further from the hall in the courtyard.

<column-break/>

When the season arrives, they are blown. In winter, the element of Water is in power. The number for Water is six. Six times seven is forty-two, which is likely why the length of the <term>yu</term> <gloss>large reed organ</gloss> is determined. The <term>sheng</term> has thirteen reeds. The <term>Guangya</term> <gloss>an ancient dictionary</gloss> says the <term>sheng</term> is made from a gourd and has thirteen pipes, with the <term>gong</term> <gloss>tonic</gloss> pipe on the left side. The <term>yu</term> reed organ symbolizes thirty-six pipes, with the <term>gong</term> pipe in the center. The <term>Litu</term> <gloss>Illustrations of Rites</gloss> says the <term>yu</term> is four feet two inches long. This <term>yu</term> has thirty-six reeds, which agrees with the <term>Litu</term>. Regarding the <term>chi</term> <gloss>bamboo flute</gloss> having seven holes, the <term>Guangya</term> says the <term>chi</term> is made of bamboo, is one foot four inches long, and has eight holes, with one hole protruding upward by one and three-tenths inches. The <term>Litu</term> says the <term>chi</term> has nine holes. <term>Zheng Sinong</term> <note>also known as Zheng Zhong, a Han scholar</note> says it has seven holes, but this is likely a scribal error and should say eight holes. Alternatively, <term>Sinong</term> may have had another source. It is said the <term>chun-du</term> <gloss>bamboo clapper</gloss> is made of bamboo five or six inches wide and seven feet long. Shorter versions are one or two feet. Its ends have two holes. The <term>zhu</term> is shaped such that it is struck against the ground with both hands; it should be six feet five inches long and contains a mallet inside.

<summary>This text describes the physical dimensions, materials, and historical commentaries regarding ancient Chinese ritual instruments including the yu scraper, sheng and yu reed organs, and the chi flute. It reconciles different classical sources on the number of reeds and holes for each instrument.</summary>
<keywords>musical instruments, Rites of Zhou, Zheng Xuan, sheng, yu, ritual music, Han dynasty commentary, organology</keywords>

It is covered with sheepskin. There are two rings attached to it. Regarding the "sparse painting" mentioned in the <term>Zheng Zhu</term> <gloss>Zheng Xuan's commentary</gloss> on the <term>Jin Che</term> <gloss>Chariot Official</gloss> concerning the red and black colors on the <term>zhu</term> <gloss>wooden percussion instrument</gloss>, the "sparse painting" refers to widely spaced lines painted upon it. <term>Zichun</term> <gloss>Zheng Zhong</gloss> reads the character <term>yuan</term> <gloss>distant</gloss> as <term>dangdi</term> <gloss>to wash/cleanse</gloss>. The reading of <term>di</term> follows the usage in the <term>Jiao Te Sheng</term> <gloss>Chapter of the Record of Rites</gloss>: "The scent and flavor are not yet formed, <term>di-di</term> <gloss>cleansed</gloss>," and this is the pronunciation of that <term>di</term>. He says the five-holed bamboo flute used today was later adopted by <term>Zheng</term> <gloss>Zheng Xuan</gloss>. "Establishing the <term>zhu</term> music" refers to the music of the <term>zhu</term> in the Xia dynasty, as the <term>Zhong Shi</term> <gloss>Bell Master</gloss> possesses this <term>zhu</term> music; because it is the same, we know what is taught here is the <term>zhu</term> music of the Xia. By saying the <term>Sheng Shi</term> <gloss>Reed-pipe Master</gloss> teaches it, it is known that the three instruments are in the courtyard. It is known they are in the courtyard. The <term>sheng</term> <gloss>mouth organ</gloss> and <term>guan</term> <gloss>bamboo pipe</gloss> are below the hall; since they are near the hall, the three instruments are also below the hall, and it is known they are in the courtyard.

<column-break/>

At the time of its sounding, the water element is active in winter, and the number for water is six. Six times seven is forty-two. The length of the <term>yu</term> <gloss>large mouth organ</gloss> likely draws from this. The <term>sheng</term> has thirteen reeds. The <term>Guangya</term> <gloss>Encyclopedia of synonyms</gloss> says the <term>sheng</term> is made from a <term>pao</term> <gloss>gourd</gloss> and has thirteen pipes, with the <term>gong</term> <gloss>tonic</gloss> pipe on the left. The <term>yu</term> represents thirty-six pipes, with the <term>gong</term> pipe in the center. The <term>Li Tu</term> <gloss>Illustrations of Rites</gloss> says the <term>yu</term> is four feet two inches long; this <term>yu</term> has thirty-six reeds, which is consistent with the <term>Li Tu</term>. The comment that the <term>chi</term> <gloss>bamboo flute</term> has seven holes—the <term>Guangya</term> says the <term>chi</term> is made of bamboo, is one foot four inches long, and has eight holes, with one hole near the top, one inch and three-tenths apart. The <term>Li Tu</term> says the <term>chi</term> has nine holes. The <term>Si Nong</term> <gloss>Agricultural Official/Commentator</gloss> says seven holes; this is likely an error by the scribe, as it should be eight holes. Perhaps the <term>Si Nong</term> had a different version. Regarding the spring <term>du</term> <gloss>percussive bamboo tube</gloss>, it is made of bamboo five or six inches in diameter and seven feet long, with shorter ones being one or two feet. Its ends have two holes. The <term>zhu</term> is shaped such that one uses both hands to strike the ground. The <term>ying</term> <gloss>percussive wooden box</gloss> is six feet five inches long, and within it is a pestle.

# The Eight Rows of Dancers and the Singing of the Yong Ode
<gloss>Note on Li: named Yu, courtesy name Guangzu, a man of Zhaowu</gloss>

Recorded Sayings: Master You speaks of the heart, Master Cheng speaks of principle, and Master Li speaks of the person. None of these captures the meaning that the Way does not function in a vacuum. Since the heart possesses this principle, preserving this heart depends on the person. Benevolence <term>ren</term> <gloss>humaneness or perfect virtue</gloss> is the complete virtue of the original heart. If a person's original good heart is preserved and not lost, then their actions will naturally have order and harmony. If this heart is once released, it is merely human desire and a selfish heart at work; how could there be order and harmony? Benevolence is simply what principle should be. Principle must be inside the human heart before one can speak of the complete word "Benevolence." 

Master Rao said: Master You explains the word "Benevolence" intimately, but the two terms "Ritual" and "Music" are not clearly distinguished. Master Cheng explains the significance of Ritual and Music, but the word "Benevolence" is not treated intimately. One must combine these two theories into one before the meanings of Benevolence, Ritual, and Music are fully provided. Master Cheng’s statement that "without it there is no order and no harmony" describes the absence of the substance of Ritual and Music. Master Li’s mention of "bells, drums, jade, and silk" describes the presence of the external form of Ritual and Music. These two theories must also be combined into one; only then is the meaning of "what can be done with Ritual and Music" fully exhausted. The Collected Commentaries utilize profound and subtle ideas; the reader must examine them carefully. Master You speaks of the substance and function of Ritual and Music; Master Cheng refers specifically to the essence of Ritual and Music.

<summary>This page contains Neo-Confucian commentaries on the relationship between inner benevolence and the external practice of ritual and music, debating the interpretations of Masters You, Cheng, and Li. It emphasizes that without a preserved moral heart, the external forms of bells, drums, and jade are meaningless.</summary>

<meta>This page appears to be a repetitive error in the source material or the transcription. After the first paragraph, the phrase "but the Record, below the word 'flute', separately mentions the Great Warrior Dance, meaning the music of the Martial Poem is also an 'Image'" repeats hundreds of times until the end of the scan.</meta>

<margin>Thirteen, Mao’s Commentary and Sub-commentary on the Odes, Imperial Edition of the Four Treasuries</margin>

Regarding these matters, the music of the *Great Warrior* <note>original: "Dawa" 大武; refers to the ritual dance of King Wu of Zhou</note> symbolizes the deeds of King Wu. Both are forms of "Images" <note>symbolic ritual dances</note>. However, the author of the Preface here mentions the performance of the *Great Warrior* and the "Image Dance" <note>original: "Xiangwu" 象舞</note>. In the section for the *Martial* <note>original: "Wu" 武; a specific poem in the Odes</note> poem, it was not possible to repeat the word "Image," so the text specifically uses the name of the music and calls it the performance of the *Great Warrior*. In reality, the music of the *Great Warrior* is also an "Image." Therefore, the *Book of Rites* in the chapters on the Crown Prince, the Hall of Distinction, and the System of Sacrifices all state: "Sing the *Pure Temple* <note>original: "Qingmiao" 清廟</note> in the upper hall, and play the 'Image' on the flutes in the lower hall." The "Image" and the *Pure Temple* are placed in opposition, and thus both are names of poems. Therefore, the commentary on the Hall of Distinction defines "Image" as the "Martial" poem of the Odes of Zhou. By calling the poem "Martial" an "Image," it is clear that the chapter on the *Great Warrior* is also an "Image." 

However, the text of the *Record* <note>the Book of Rites</note> below the word "flute" separately mentions the performance of the *Great Warrior Dance* <note>original: "舞大武"</note>, meaning the music of the *Martial* poem is also an "Image." <note>The remaining text on this page consists of the preceding clause "but the text of the Record below the word 'flute' separately mentions the performance of the Great Warrior Dance, meaning the music of the Martial poem is also an 'Image'" repeated without variation hundreds of times.</note>

<summary>This page discusses the ritual terminology and classification of Zhou Dynasty sacrificial music, specifically identifying the Great Warrior dance and the Martial poem as synonymous with the term Image. The page contains a significant repetitive error where a single explanatory clause is printed hundreds of times.</summary>
<keywords>Great Warrior, Image Dance, Book of Rites, Odes of Zhou, King Wu, ritual music, Pure Temple</keywords>

<margin>Imperially commissioned Siku Quanshu, Mao Shi Zhushu, Volume 13</margin>

...the affairs of King Wu, and the music of the Great Martial Dance <note>original: "大武"</note> represents the affairs of King Wu. Both are intended as representations. However, the preface here says "Performing the Great Martial Dance, the dance representing the martial deeds" in the section on the "Wu" poem <note>refers to the *Zhou Song* poem "Wu"</note>. It cannot repeat the phrase "performing the representation," so it indicates the name of the music by saying "performing the Great Martial Dance." In reality, the music of the Great Martial Dance also acts as a representation. Therefore, the *Liji* <note>Book of Rites</note>—in the chapters "Wen Wang Shi Zi," "Ming Tang Wei," and "Ji Tong"—all say, "Singing 'Qing Miao' <note>a poem in the Zhou Song</note> while ascending, and playing the *Xiang* <note>a type of dance music</note> with lower-register pipes." *Xiang* and *Qing Miao* are paired, meaning both are poems. Thus, the annotation on "Ming Tang Wei" explains that the *Xiang* refers to the "Wu" poem of the *Zhou Song*. It means the "Wu" poem is the *Xiang*, making it clear that the section of the Great Martial Dance is also a representation. However, the text of the *Liji* separately mentions "dancing the Great Martial Dance" after mentioning the pipes. This means the music for the "Wu" poem is also a representation.

<summary>This passage clarifies the terminology used to describe the "Great Martial Dance" music and its relationship to the "Wu" poem within the *Zhou Song*, reconciling discrepancies between the preface and the *Book of Rites*.</summary>
<keywords>Mao Shi Zhushu, Great Martial Dance, Da Wu, Zhou Song, Liji, music, ritual, representation</keywords>

<margin>
呂氏家塾讀詩記
</margin>

曰南山. 鎬京之陽終南之山也 孔氏曰如竹之叢

生根本之衆 <gloss>董氏曰苞叢生而固也</gloss> 鄭氏曰式用也 歐陽

氏曰猶圖也謀也 董氏曰宣王作室後臨水前對

山. 其盤基之厚如竹之苞其締蔭之廣如松之茂 <gloss>朱氏曰其下之固如竹之苞其上之密如松之茂</gloss> 兄及弟矣式相好矣無相猶

矣. 所謂聚國族於斯也 李氏曰兄弟之居此室各

相和好輯睦無有相圖 朱氏曰蓋頌禱之辭 <gloss>吕氏曰保</gloss>

吾兄弟於斯繼吾祖妣於斯安吾身於斯傳吾子孫

於斯. 故曰兄及弟矣式相好矣無相猶矣又曰似續

translations.T1:
It says Southern Mountain <note>original: 南山</note>. This refers to Mount Zhongnan <note>original: 終南之山</note>, located on the sunny southern side of the capital, Haojing. Master Kong <note>Kong Yingda</note> says that just as bamboo grows in thickets, its roots are numerous and tightly clustered. <gloss>Master Dong says that the thicket grows clustered and firm.</gloss> Master Zheng <note>Zheng Xuan</note> says that <term>shi</term> <gloss>式</gloss> means to use. Master Ouyang <note>Ouyang Xiu</note> says it is like plotting or planning. Master Dong says that when King Xuan built this palace, it faced the water behind and the mountains in front. The thickness of its foundation is like the clustering of bamboo, and the breadth of its shade is like the luxuriance of pine trees. <gloss>Master Zhu <note>Zhu Xi</note> says the firmness of its lower part is like bamboo clusters; the density of its upper part is like the luxuriance of pines.</gloss> Elder brothers and younger brothers shall love one another, and they shall not plot against each other. This is what is meant by "gathering the clans of the state in this place." Master Li says that when brothers reside in this house, they each harmonize in peace and concord, without any mutual scheming. Master Zhu says these are words of praise and prayer. <gloss>Master Lü <note>Lü Zuqian</note> says:</gloss> My brothers are preserved in this place; I succeed my ancestors in this place; I find peace for my person in this place; and I pass this on to my descendants in this place. Therefore it is said: "Elder brothers and younger brothers shall love one another, and they shall not plot against each other," and it is also said "to continue the line."

<summary>This page provides classical commentary on the poem Si Gan from the Classic of Poetry, focusing on metaphors of bamboo and pine to describe the stability of King Xuan's palace and the necessity of brotherly harmony.</summary>
<keywords>Classic of Poetry, Shijing, Mount Zhongnan, King Xuan of Zhou, family harmony, architectural metaphors, Lü Zuqian</keywords>
translations.T2:
<margin>Lü's Family School Commentary on the Classic of Poetry</margin>

Regarding "the southern mountains": This refers to Mount Zhongnan to the south of Haojing. Master Kong said, "It is like a cluster of bamboo."

Regarding "growing at the root in great numbers" <gloss>Master Dong said: "Bao" (苞) means to grow in a cluster and be firm.</gloss> Master Zheng said: "Shi" (式) means to use. Master Ouyang said: "It is like planning or deliberating." Master Dong said: "King Xuan built this hall with water in front and the mountain facing the rear. Its foundation is as thick as a cluster of bamboo, and its overhead shade is as lush as a pine tree." <gloss>Master Zhu said: "Its base is as firm as a cluster of bamboo, and its upper canopy is as dense as a flourishing pine."</gloss> "Elder brothers and younger brothers, may you be in harmony with each other; let there be no schemes against one another." This is what is called gathering the state and the clans here. Master Li said: "The brothers dwell in this room, each in harmony and concord, without any scheming against each other." Master Zhu said: "This is a prayer of praise." <gloss>Master Lü said: "To protect our brothers here, to continue our ancestors here, to settle our bodies here, and to transmit this to our descendants here."</gloss> Therefore, it says, "Elder brothers and younger brothers, may you be in harmony with each other; let there be no schemes against one another." It further says, "to resemble and to continue."

<summary>This page provides classical commentary on the "Si Gan" poem from the Classic of Poetry, focusing on the metaphorical description of a palace's architecture and the ethical expectation for harmony among brothers.</summary>
<keywords>Lü's Family School, Classic of Poetry, Si Gan, Mount Zhongnan, King Xuan, harmony, lineage</keywords>

Its foundation was as thick as a bamboo clump, and its widespread shade was as lush as a pine tree." <gloss>Master Zhu said, "Its lower part is as firm as a bamboo clump, and its upper part is as dense as a pine tree."</gloss> "Brothers and their siblings, they should love each other and not plot against each other." This refers to gathering the nation's clans here. Master Li said, "Brothers living in this house should be harmonious and amicable, without plotting against each other." Master Zhu said, "This is a hymn of prayer." <gloss>Master Lü said, "To protect"</gloss> my brothers here, to continue my ancestors here, to find peace for myself here, and to pass it on to my descendants here. Therefore, it says, "Brothers and their siblings, they should love each other and not plot against each other." It also says, "continuation."

<summary>This page contains a detailed commentary by various scholars (Kong, Dong, Zheng, Ouyang, Zhu, Li, Lü) on specific lines from the poem "Si Gan" from the Classic of Poetry. The commentary focuses on the symbolism of mountains and plants, emphasizing the themes of stability, harmony, and familial continuity within the context of King Xuan's palace and the importance of brotherly affection.</summary>

The Emperor issued an edict following this advice. In the eighth year of the <term>Kaiyuan</term> <gloss>713–741 AD</gloss> era, Li Yuanguan, the <term>Guozi Siye</term> <gloss>Vice Chancellor of the Imperial Academy</gloss>, submitted a memorial stating: "The Former Sage, Father Xuan <note>A posthumous title for Confucius</note>, is accompanied in the seating arrangement by the Former Teacher, Master Yan <note>Yan Hui</note>. Master Yan's Way was second only to those born with innate knowledge, and his talents shone as one who had entered the master's private quarters. I request that according to the text of the Rites, he should be seated in attendance. Furthermore, the disciples of the four disciplines, such as Min Ziqian and others, were all devoted to the Confucian arts and personally received the holy teachings. Although their statues are displayed, they do not participate in the sacrificial offerings. According to the records of He Xiu and others, even lesser figures receive some portion of the shared sacrifices; how is it that the disciples who 'ascended the hall and entered the room' alone do not receive the remaining offerings? I request that during the spring and autumn <term>Shidian</term> <gloss>Sacrificial Offerings to Confucius</gloss> ceremonies, they be included in the offerings. I also ask that the authorities be ordered to paint their images on the walls and compose eulogies for them."

The imperial edict stated: "Seated statues should be made for the ten people including Master Yan, and they shall all be included in the shared sacrifices. Zeng Shen, whose great filial piety and virtue were supreme among his peers, shall have a special statue sculpted and seated next to the Ten Philosophers. The seventy disciples and twenty-two worthy men shall be painted on the temple walls. As Master Yan is the Second Sage, I shall personally compose and write the eulogy for his ceremonial robes."

<summary>This page discusses the historical practices and significance of the <term>di</term> and <term>xia</term> imperial ancestral sacrifices in ancient China, particularly concerning the joint feasting of ancestral spirit tablets, the timing of these rituals, and their symbolic meaning in establishing familial hierarchy and remembering ancestors.</summary>

The spirit tablets of those whose temples have been abolished, as well as those whose temples have not been abolished, are all ascended to be offered food at the Temple of the Grand Progenitor <note>original: "太祖" <term>Taizu</term>, referring to the founding ancestor of the dynasty.</note> every five years, during which two great sacrificial rites are performed.

Under the old Han system, a <term>di</term> <gloss>great ancestral sacrifice</gloss> was performed every three years. The tablets of abolished temples were offered food at the High Temple <note>original: "高廟" <term>Gaomiao</term>, the temple dedicated to the founding emperor of the Han.</note>, while the tablets of extant temples were never included in this joint sacrifice. In the fifth year of the Yuanshi era, the <term>di</term> sacrifice was first established. Previously, eighteen years prior, the Emperor personally visited Chang'an and also performed this rite. 

The term <term>di</term> implies <term>ti</term> <gloss>to clarify/define</gloss>; it serves to clarify the order of the <term>zhaomu</term> <gloss>the ancestral rank and seating order</gloss> and the principles of superior and inferior. The <term>di</term> sacrifice is performed in the fourth month of summer. Summer is the time when the yang energy is above and the yin energy is below; thus, it rectifies the order of superior and inferior. The <term>di</term> sacrifice is also performed in the tenth month of winter. Winter is when the five grains have matured and all things are prepared; thus, the rite is completed by gathering together to consume food and drink. This code has been abandoned for eight years; I request that it be implemented according to the rites in a timely manner.

### Great Di and Small Di
<term>Li Wai Zhuan</term> <gloss>External Commentary on the Rites</gloss>: <term>Di</term> and <term>di</term>. The fixed resolution was followed by the Emperor, and from this point, the <term>di</term> was settled.

Whether great or small, the <term>Spring and Autumn Annals</term> <gloss>a Confucian classic</gloss> records the <term>di</term> but does not mention the <term>di</term> of abolished temples. There is no set time for the sacrifice to abolished temples, but there are two great sacrificial rites every five years. ### Joint Offering at the Temple of the Grand Progenitor
<term>Baihu Tong</term> <gloss>Comprehensive Discussions in the White Tiger Hall</gloss>: The <term>di</term> is the ritual where the tablets of abolished temples are all brought together to be offered food at the Temple of the Grand Progenitor.

According to the <term>Wujing Tongyi</term> <gloss>General Principles of the Five Classics</gloss>: For kings and feudal lords, an intercalary month occurs every three years. The way of Heaven is then small-scale and complete, so a <term>xia</term> <gloss>joint sacrificial rite</gloss> is performed every three years. A <term>xia</term> involves taking the tablets of those whose temples have not yet been moved and offering them food together in the Temple of the Grand Progenitor. Every five years, there are two intercalary months. The way of Heaven is then large-scale and complete, so a <term>di</term> is performed every five years. <summary>This page discusses the historical protocols for the <term>di</term> and <term>xia</term> sacrificial rites in ancient China, specifically detailing when and how ancestral tablets were moved or consolidated at the Temple of the Grand Progenitor to maintain proper hierarchical order.</summary>

The ancestral tablets from both destroyed temples and those not yet destroyed are all brought together to share in the offerings to the Great Ancestor <note>the founding progenitor of the dynasty</note>. Every five years, the Great Sacrifice <term>Yinji</term> <gloss>an abundant, grand ancestral rite</gloss> is performed twice. Under the old system of the Han dynasty, the <term>Di</term> <gloss>major quinquennial ancestral sacrifice</gloss> was performed once every three years; the tablets from destroyed temples shared in the offerings at the Temple of the High Ancestor, while tablets from extant temples were not included in this collective sacrifice. In the fifth year of the Yuanshi era <note>5 AD</note>, the <term>Di</term> sacrifice was first established. Eighteen years prior to that, when the Emperor personally visited Chang'an, he also performed this rite. The term <term>Di</term> <gloss>sacrificial rite</gloss> carries the meaning of <term>Di</term> <gloss>to examine or determine</gloss>, specifically to determine the proper order of <term>Zhaomu</term> <gloss>the chronological arrangement of ancestral tablets by generations</gloss> and the ranks of honor and status. The <term>Di</term> sacrifice is held in the fourth month of summer. In summer, the <term>Yang</term> energy is above and the <term>Yin</term> energy is below, which serves to rectify the principles of honor and status. The <term>Di</term> sacrifice is also held in the tenth month of winter. In winter, the five grains have ripened and all goods are prepared, so the ritual is complete; thus, the people gather together to eat and drink. These ceremonies have been neglected for eight years. It is requested that they be implemented according to the ritual protocols in a timely manner.

### The Great and Small Di Sacrifices

The *External Commentary on the Book of Rites* <note>original: "Li Waizhuan"</note> states that the <term>Di</term> sacrifice establishes fixed discussions. The Emperor followed this, and from then on, the <term>Di</term> sacrifice was settled. There are Great <term>Di</term> and Small <term>Di</term> sacrifices. In the classics of the *Spring and Autumn Annals*, the <term>Di</term> sacrifice is recorded, but not the specific distinction of the Small <term>Di</term>. Destroyed temples do not receive seasonal sacrifices, but every five years there are two Great Sacrifices. When a divine tablet first enters the temple, a <term>Di</term> sacrifice is performed for it. In the spring of the following year, another <term>Di</term> sacrifice is held.

### Collective Offerings to the Great Ancestor

The *Comprehensive Discussions in the White Tiger Hall* <note>original: "Baihu Tong"</note> states that the <term>Di</term> sacrifice is when the tablets from the destroyed temples are all brought together to share in the offerings to the Great Ancestor. According to the *General Meaning of the Five Classics*, Kings and Dukes have a leap month every three years, representing the minor completion of the Way of Heaven. Therefore, every three years the <term>Xia</term> <gloss>collective ancestral sacrifice</gloss> is held. The <term>Xia</term> sacrifice involves taking the tablets from temples that have not yet been moved to share in the offerings within the temple of the Great Ancestor. Every five years there are two leap months, representing the great completion of the Way of Heaven. Therefore, every five years the <term>Di</term> sacrifice is held. The <term>Di</term> sacrifice involves taking the tablets from temples that have already been moved and bringing them together for offerings in the temple. This is done to avoid forgetting the lineage of the ancestors. It maintains the succession by moving from the close relatives to the distant ones, ensuring the ancestors are not forgotten. It further states that the <term>Di</term> sacrifice reaches even those in the moved temples because it is impossible for every generation to succeed the ruler <note>referring to the limitation on how many generations of individual temples are maintained before tablets are moved to a collective space</note>.

<summary>This page discusses the historical and ritual significance of the Di and Xia ancestral sacrifices, detailing the timing of these rites and the collective offering of ancestral tablets to the Great Ancestor.</summary>
<keywords>ancestral rites, Di sacrifice, Xia sacrifice, Great Ancestor, Han dynasty ritual, Zhaomu order, temple tablets</keywords>

Supplement: *Records of Shu* <note>the historical chronicle of the Shu Han dynasty</note>: Mi Zhu, courtesy name Zizhong, was a native of Donghai. For generations, his family had traded in goods and accumulated wealth, with ten thousand servants and assets worth hundreds of millions. When Lü Bu later raided and defeated the First Sovereign, capturing his wife and children, Mi Zhu offered his own sister as a wife to the First Sovereign and provided two thousand soldiers along with gold, silk, and currency to support the army. The army's prestige relied on this and was restored. Later, when the Former Lord pacified Yizhou, Mi Zhu was appointed General Who Pacifies Han. His younger brother, Fang, served as the Grand Administrator of Nan Commandery, but he defected and welcomed Sun Quan, leading to Guan Yu's defeat. Mi Zhu pleaded guilty, but the Former Lord treated him as before, stating that brothers should not be held accountable for each other's actions.

Imperial Selection of the Deep Mirror of Categorized Letters

Autumn Rabbit's Quill <note>This refers to the fine hair of a rabbit's coat in autumn, often used to make high-quality brushes.</note> Added from the Records of Shu <note>original: "Shu Zhi"</note>: Mi Zhu, whose courtesy name was Zizhong, was a native of Donghai. His family had traded in goods for generations, employing ten thousand servants and laborers, and his wealth was valued at hundreds of millions. Tao Qian, the Governor of Xu Province, recruited him as an Attendant Officer. When Tao Qian died, Mi Zhu was ordered to welcome the Former Lord <note>referring to Liu Bei</note> to govern the province. Later, when Lu Bu launched a surprise attack and defeated the Former Lord, capturing his wife and children, Mi Zhu presented his younger sister to become the Former Lord's wife. He also assisted the military with two thousand people and vast quantities of gold, silk, and currency. The prestige of the army relied on this support to rise once more. After the Former Lord settled Yi Province, he appointed Mi Zhu as General Who Settles the Han. Mi Zhu's younger brother, Mi Fang, served as the Grand Administrator of Nanjun, but he became disloyal and welcomed Sun Quan, which led to the defeat of Guan Yu. Mi Zhu requested to be punished for his brother's actions, but the Former Lord held that brothers should not be held responsible for one another and treated him with the same favor as before. Originally mentioned: Also Liu Yan, whose courtesy name was Weishuo, was enfeoffed as the Marquis of Duxiang. His clothing, carriages, food, and drink were extravagant and wasteful. He kept dozens of maidservants, all of whom were trained in vocal music. Records of Wu <note>original: "Wu Zhi"</note>: He Qi was by nature extravagant and fond of military affairs. The boats he traveled in were intricately carved and painted in red, featuring green canopies and crimson eaves.

<summary>This page records the lives of Mi Zhu and other officials from the Three Kingdoms period, highlighting Mi Zhu's immense wealth and loyalty to Liu Bei despite his brother's betrayal. It also notes the extravagant lifestyles of Liu Yan and He Qi.</summary>
